# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## A required correction to this guide's premise

The request states that Massachusetts did not require vital registration until 1841 and therefore "nothing civil exists" for 1820–1850. The FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Vital Records page contradicts this directly: town-level recording was required by law **from 1639**, though not all places complied consistently. The 1841 act created the first unified **statewide** collection system — not the first civil records. FamilySearch's volume search confirmed a digitized Berkshire County volume (image group 004500891) explicitly labeled "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," covering **1761–1850** — a civil record series spanning the entire target window. Church registers and cemetery inscriptions are valuable and often fuller than town entries (particularly before compliance improved after 1841), but they are not the only records. The guide below covers all record types.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761 (from Hampshire County)
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Geographic note:** Berkshire County is bounded by New York on the west and Vermont on the north — families in this region regularly crossed both state lines for church membership, land purchase, marriage, and burial.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start dates:** Town-level recording was required by law from 1639. Statewide consolidated recording began in 1841. Boston did not appear in the statewide system until 1850 (a tougher regulation that year), though Boston recorded locally throughout. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).
- **What exists:** Town clerk vital record volumes covering births, marriages, and deaths exist at the town level across the entire 1820–1850 window, not only after 1841. FamilySearch has digitized a Berkshire County town clerk vital and town records volume (image group 004500891, 512 images) covering 1761–1850.
- **Where held — originals:** With the clerk of the town or city where the event occurred.
- **Where held — online/compiled:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (3,456,789 records) is a name-indexed statewide compilation at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 and covers the target period. Published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" abstracts exist for over 200 Massachusetts towns — check whether the specific Berkshire County town is in the series; NEHGS holds the compiled series.
- **Marriage intentions:** Recorded in the bride's home town; additional copies may appear in the groom's home town and their current place of residence. Search all three if the couple came from different places.
- **Gaps:** Not all towns maintained records consistently before 1841. Volume 004500891 is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Digitization level:** Collection 2061550 — indexed + images. Volume 004500891 — browse-only images.

---

### Church Records

- **Denominations confirmed:** Congregational (Pittsfield), confirmed by FamilySearch volume 004500892. Other denominations were present in Berkshire County during 1820–1850 but are not specifically named in tool results from this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (a proxy for birth), marriages, burials (a proxy for death), and confirmations — a separate dated event that may appear years after the baptism entry.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (987,654 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. FamilySearch also holds a digitized Pittsfield Congregational Church Records volume (image group 004500892, 274 images, 1791–1850) — browse-only. For denominations not in collection 1921657, consult the denomination's own archives and NEHGS.
- **Gaps:** Only the Pittsfield Congregational volume is confirmed as a Berkshire County-specific digitized volume in this survey. Registers for Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, Quaker, Dutch Reformed, and other denominations active in western Massachusetts in this period are not confirmed as online from tool results.

---

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, 1840 (heads of household only; other members listed by age group and sex only); 1850 (first census to name every household member including children, with age, birthplace, and occupation). The 1850 census is the first that permits direct identification of children born 1820–1850 by name.
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census for the 1820–1850 period was confirmed by tool results.
- **Access:** U.S. Federal Census available via Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate), estate inventories, guardianship files. If a person died without a will (intestate), search the administration series rather than the wills series.
- **Date range:** Massachusetts probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts and survive through the target period.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Probate Court (Pittsfield). FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (567,890 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901.
- **Digitization level:** Collection 1678901 — indexed + images.

---

### Land Records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state; no General Land Office patents apply).
- **Date range:** From 1761 for Berkshire County; earlier grants may be in Hampshire County records.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds (Pittsfield). Massachusetts land records "survive in remarkably complete runs" per wiki search results.

---

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (service ended 1815; pension files, bounty land warrants, and widow's pensions are active research targets for the 1820–1850 period); Revolutionary War (pension files active for older family members throughout this window).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal service and pension records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has military record digitization. Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds Massachusetts militia rolls.

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the main online index for cemetery inscriptions. Cemetery transcriptions are a valuable source for death dates and family groupings, particularly for the 1820–1841 period before statewide vital registration began.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries or town offices; not confirmed as digitized from this survey's tool results.

---

### Newspaper Records

- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for historical newspapers online.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices in local papers can substitute for or supplement missing vital record entries, especially in the gap before 1841 statewide registration.

---

### Immigration/Naturalization Records

- **Relevant ports:** Berkshire County is an inland county; nearest ports of entry were Boston and New York City.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1784312, "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (1,234,567 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312. FamilySearch collection 1459213, "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (345,678 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213. NARA for originals.

---

### Tax Records

- **Types:** Town and county property tax lists; poll taxes.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household and can substitute for intercensal years or missing vital records. A person who appears and then drops from the tax list may indicate death, departure, or coming of age.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) and local town offices; not confirmed as online from tool results.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch — collection 2061550 | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 | Town clerk vital records 1820–1850, pre- and post-statewide act | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 |
| FamilySearch — collection 1921657 | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 | Baptism, marriage, burial registers | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 |
| FamilySearch — collection 1678901 | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 | Wills, administrations, inventories | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 |
| FamilySearch — collection 1784312 | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 | Immigration arrivals | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 |
| FamilySearch — collection 1459213 | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 | Pre-1906 naturalizations | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213 |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 enumerations | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records | Cemetery inscriptions, death events not in town records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Service records, pension index | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | Federal service/pension, immigration originals | Pension and bounty land files; passenger list originals | In-person / online request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned exactly 2 digitized volumes matching Berkshire County for 1820–1850. Both are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). The five statewide FamilySearch collections above include Berkshire County material and are name-indexed.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Berkshire County town and city clerks | Original town clerk vital record books — the creating authority for pre-1841 civil records | In-person or written request to the specific town clerk |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Wills, administrations, guardianships from 1761 | In-person or mail request |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deed books from 1761; remarkably complete per wiki search result | In-person or mail request |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony/state records; militia rolls; statewide vital records submitted post-1841 | In-person or online request |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in the region; "Vital Records to 1850" published series | In-person or NEHGS membership |
| Individual church archives and denominational offices | Original parish registers for denominations not yet digitized | Direct contact with congregation or diocese/conference |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Town clerk vital record volume (image group 004500891):** Berkshire County town clerk vital and town records, 1761–1850, are digitized on FamilySearch but are browse-only — 512 images must be browsed without any name index.
- **Church registers beyond Pittsfield Congregational:** Only the Pittsfield Congregational volume (image group 004500892) is confirmed as Berkshire County-specific in this survey. Registers of Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, Quaker, and other denominations are not confirmed as online from tool results.
- **Tax records:** Not confirmed as online from tool results.
- **Sexton and burial registers:** Not confirmed as online from tool results.
- **Massachusetts militia records (1812 era):** Not confirmed as online from tool results.
- **Cemetery stone inscriptions beyond Find A Grave:** Transcription projects are physical or held at local historical societies; extent of online coverage not confirmed from tool results.

---

## Known Record Losses

No specific record losses for Berkshire County were returned by any tool result in this survey. The absence of a reported loss should not be read as a guarantee that all records survive; check with individual town clerks and the Massachusetts Archives for the status of any specific town series before concluding a record is missing.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Town clerk records are the first stop, not a fallback.** Because Massachusetts required town-level recording from 1639, the town clerk series is the primary civil source for births, marriages, and deaths throughout 1820–1850. Begin with FamilySearch collection 2061550 (name-indexed) and then browse volume 004500891 for entries the index may have missed.

2. **Marriage intentions appear in multiple towns.** Record the bride's home town and the groom's home town separately: each may hold an independent intention entry that the other does not.

3. **The "Vital Records to 1850" published series** exists for over 200 Massachusetts towns. These printed abstracts are often the fastest path into the pre-1841 record mass for a specific Berkshire County town; check NEHGS for which towns are covered.

4. **Cross-border research is essential for this family.** Families in northwestern and western Berkshire County regularly crossed into New York and Vermont for church membership, land purchase, marriage, and burial. Town clerk vital records, church registers, deeds, and probate records may exist on both sides of both state lines for the same family. This survey covers Massachusetts only — run separate locality surveys for the adjacent New York and Vermont jurisdictions before concluding a record does not exist.

5. **The 1850 census as a naming bridge.** The 1820, 1830, and 1840 federal censuses name only the head of household; children and other members appear only as tallies. The 1850 census names every member. Use the 1850 enumeration to establish children's names and then trace their births backward through town clerk records and church registers.

6. **Probate is a relationship source.** Wills and estate inventories name heirs, spouses, and children by name and often give relationships — probate records fill gaps when vital records are absent or silent.

7. **Identify the specific town first.** Which Berkshire County town the family lived in determines which town clerk book and which church registers to request. Once the town is known, run a targeted search of FamilySearch collection 2061550 and browse volume 004500891 before moving to church registers.

- **Cross-border research is essential for this family.** The request places the family close to both the New York and Vermont state lines. Families in northwestern and western Berkshire County regularly crossed into New York and Vermont for church membership, land purchase, marriage, and burial. Town clerk vital records, church registers, deeds, and probate records may exist on both sides of both state lines for the same family. This survey covers Massachusetts only; run separate locality surveys for the adjacent New York and Vermont jurisdictions before concluding a record does not exist.

The 1850 census names every member. Use the 1850 enumeration to establish children's names and then trace their births backward through town clerk records and church registers.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Principal town:** Bushmills
- **Church of Ireland diocese:** Connor; Roman Catholic diocese: Down and Connor
- **Religious composition:** Predominantly Ulster Scots (Scots-Irish) Presbyterian in the Bushmills/Route district; also Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic, and a small Methodist presence
- **Key events:** 1798 Rebellion; Act of Union 1800; Great Famine 1845–1852 (significant emigration, though less severe than the west); railway expansion 1850s–60s

---

## Record Types Available

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

| Event type | Coverage begins | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Catholic marriages | 1 April 1845 | GRO Northern Ireland, Belfast |
| All births, deaths, Catholic marriages | 1 January 1864 | GRO Northern Ireland, Belfast |

**Practical implication:** Almost all vital events in your 1780–1870 target window fall *before* civil registration and are found only in church registers. Civil registration covers only the last six years of the window for births and deaths.

Online access: **IrishGenealogy.ie** (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) — free, indexes and many images.

---

### Church Records — Priority Source for a Presbyterian Family

The Bushmills/Billy area falls within the **Route Presbytery** of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland. The congregations most likely to hold registers for a family in Billy civil parish are:

- **Bushmills Presbyterian Church** (Route Presbytery) — seated in the principal town
- **Dervock Presbyterian Church** — served parts of the surrounding rural area
- **Ballybogy and Kilraghts** — wider Route district, may be relevant depending on townland

**Step before searching registers:** Identify the specific townland in Billy parish from Griffith's Valuation or the Tithe Applotment Books, then contact the **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland** to confirm which congregation served that townland and what dates its registers begin. Some congregational registers start only in the 1820s or 1830s.

**Where Presbyterian registers are held:**
- **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland**, Church House, Fisherwick Place, Belfast BT1 6DW (originals and deposit copies)
- **PRONI** (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ — microfilm copies of many registers; eCatalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni

**Church of Ireland:** Billy parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) — originals at PRONI or the **Representative Church Body Library** (RCB Library), Dublin; many are on IrishGenealogy.ie.

**Roman Catholic:** Diocese of Down and Connor; registers typically begin 1820s–1840s for north Antrim. Microfilm at the National Library of Ireland, Dublin; many indexed on IrishGenealogy.ie and Ancestry.

**Note on the 1922 fire:** Presbyterian registers were generally held locally and survived. Many Church of Ireland registers that had been deposited in Dublin were destroyed (see Known Record Losses).

---

### Census Records and Substitutes

**Irish census records for 1780–1870 are almost entirely lost.** The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 returns were largely destroyed in the 1922 PRO Dublin fire; the 1861 and 1871 returns were deliberately destroyed by government order.

**Census substitutes — these are your primary population-level sources:**

| Source | Dates | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | All occupiers of tithable land; Billy parish is covered | Free: titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie; also Ancestry, FamilySearch |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** | c. 1858–1864 | All occupiers of property; most detailed mid-century substitute | Free: AskAboutIreland.ie / Griffith's Valuation Online |
| **Flaxseed Premium List (1796)** | 1796 | County Antrim linen weavers — directly applicable for a Presbyterian Route family | Ancestry; various indexes |
| **Poor Law rate books** | From 1838 | All ratable occupiers, annually — fills the census gap | PRONI (physical) |
| **1901 and 1911 census** | 1901, 1911 | Complete survivors; outside your window but essential for identifying survivors | Free: census.nationalarchives.ie |

---

### Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837** and **Griffith's Valuation c. 1858–1864** — see above; both are land records as well as census substitutes
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of deeds, mortgages, and leases registered voluntarily; a leasing family may appear — indexes on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Estate papers at PRONI:** Much of north Antrim was held by a small number of landed estates; rent rolls and tenancy agreements are an underused source for tenant families. PRONI's eCatalogue lists estate papers by parish and townland.
- **Poor Law rate books:** Ballymoney Poor Law Union (and possibly Coleraine Union depending on townland) — PRONI.

---

### Probate Records

- **Before 1858:** Probate was proved in the Consistorial Court of Connor. These records were largely destroyed in the 1922 fire. The **Inland Revenue Betham Abstracts** (National Archives of Ireland) provide partial pre-1858 coverage.
- **From 1858:** Probate transferred to the **Belfast District Probate Registry**. Annual calendars of grants (indexes) from 1858 survive and are online at the National Archives of Ireland. Original wills 1858–1900 were largely destroyed in 1922; the calendars name the deceased, address, occupation, estate value, and executor.

---

### Military Records

Relevant conflicts: 1798 Rebellion, Napoleonic Wars 1803–1815, Crimean War 1854–1856.
- **British Army service records:** The National Archives, Kew (series WO); many on Findmypast and Ancestry. Note: a 1931 War Office fire destroyed a large portion of pre-1920 service records for other ranks.
- **Pension records (Chelsea Pensioners):** The National Archives, Kew; on Findmypast.
- **County Antrim Militia:** Some records at PRONI.

---

### Newspapers

- ***Belfast Newsletter*** (from 1737) — the major regional paper; marriage and death notices for County Antrim throughout the period
- ***Coleraine Chronicle*** (from 1844) — covers north Antrim including Bushmills
- **Access:** British Newspaper Archive (subscription, https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk); PRONI microfilm

---

### Immigration/Emigration

North Antrim was a major emigration source throughout this period — to North America in the 1780s–1800s, to Canada (New Brunswick, Ontario) in the 1820s–1840s, intensifying during and after the Famine. Principal departure ports: Londonderry/Derry and Belfast.
- US passenger lists (post-1820): Ancestry, FamilySearch
- Canadian lists: Library and Archives Canada (bac-lac.gc.ca)
- Ulster Historical Foundation emigration databases; PRONI emigration records

---

### Cemetery Records

- Church of Ireland and Presbyterian churchyard gravestone inscriptions are the most accessible burial record for this period
- Many north Antrim transcriptions are on Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves (billiongraves.com)
- Ulster Historical Foundation has published gravestone surveys
- PRONI holds some gravestone transcripts

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Church registers (original and microfilm), estate papers, court records, Poor Law records, land records for County Antrim | In-person; some records via PRONI online service; eCatalogue free at nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast** | Presbyterian congregational registers, Route Presbytery records | In-person by appointment |
| **GRO Northern Ireland, Belfast** | Civil registration registers from 1845/1864 | In-person; indexes and images at IrishGenealogy.ie (free) |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** | Census fragments, probate calendars 1858+, school records, Tithe Books | In-person; many indexes free online |
| **National Library of Ireland, Dublin** | Catholic registers (microfilm), Griffith's notebooks, newspapers | In-person; microfilm registers online |
| **RCB Library, Dublin** | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person by appointment |
| **The National Archives, Kew** | British Army service, pension, militia records | In-person; many records on Findmypast/Ancestry |

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1922 PRO Dublin fire:** Destroyed most pre-1858 wills and administration bonds; most of the 1821–1851 census returns; many Church of Ireland registers that had been deposited in Dublin. **Presbyterian registers were generally held locally and were not destroyed.**
- **Government destruction of 1861 and 1871 census returns:** No names survive.
- **1931 War Office fire:** Destroyed a large portion of British Army service records for other ranks serving before 1920.

---

## Recommended First Steps for Your 1825 Billy Parish Family

1. **Identify the specific townland** using Griffith's Primary Valuation (c. 1858–1864) at AskAboutIreland.ie and the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) at the National Archives of Ireland — the townland is the key that unlocks every other record class.
2. **Search the 1796 Flaxseed Premium List** — for a Presbyterian linen-weaving family in the Route area it may name the grandparents' generation.
3. **Contact the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland** to confirm which Route Presbytery congregation served that townland and the start date of its surviving registers.
4. **Search the Route Presbytery congregation registers** at PRONI (microfilm) or the Presbyterian Historical Society — baptisms and marriages are your best hope for pre-1864 vital events.
5. **Check the Ballymoney (and possibly Coleraine) Poor Law Union rate books at PRONI** (from 1838) for annual household listings that fill the census gap.
6. **Cross the county line into County Londonderry/Derry** — the western townlands of Billy parish are close to Coleraine; some families used Coleraine-area churches, registered in Coleraine district, or lived on both sides of the boundary.

---

Check the FamilySearch catalog directly at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog for County Antrim, Ireland, collections.*

Put together a locality guide for Billy parish for roughly 1780-1870: which record types are available, where they are held, and which church registers would cover a Presbyterian family there.

Every Ireland-specific page returned by both the FamilySearch Wiki tool and Wikipedia search is producing the same generic fallback page — the wiki-query-api is not serving Ireland pages in this environment. I will note that outage throughout the guide and add the required quirk. Place-search also returned no results for any form of Irish place names, so collections_search, volume_search, and external_links_search cannot be called. The guide below is built on established Irish genealogical practice; specific collection IDs, record counts, and digitization percentages that must come from tool results are marked as unverified — re-run this guide once the tools are operational to fill those gaps.

---

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Principal town:** Bushmills (home of the licensed distillery from 1608; a small market and fishing town throughout this period)
- **Church of Ireland diocese:** Connor (Diocese of Down and Connor for Roman Catholics)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, under the Parliament of Ireland until 1 January 1801, then the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland under the Act of Union
- **Population:** This survey could not retrieve population figures — the place_search tool returned no results for Irish places and the FamilySearch Wiki was unreachable during this survey (see quirks below)
- **Economy:** Linen weaving, fishing, farming, and distilling; the domestic linen industry was in transition to factory production by mid-century
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Ulster Scots (Scots-Irish) of Presbyterian background in the Route area; smaller Church of Ireland (Anglican) population and an older native Irish Catholic minority
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian (dominant in the Bushmills/Route district), Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic, and a small Methodist presence
- **Key historical events:** 1798 United Irishmen Rebellion; Act of Union 1800; Great Famine 1845–1852 (less severe in north Antrim than the west but significant emigration); railway expansion in the 1850s-60s

## Boundary changes

- **Barony of Cary** remained stable throughout this period; Billy parish boundaries were unchanged
- **Pre-1801:** Records generated under the Parliament of Ireland, though for County Antrim the administrative picture was similar
- **Post-1858:** Probate jurisdiction shifted from ecclesiastical courts to the new Principal Registry and district registries (see Probate section)
- **Post-1864:** Civil registration of all vital events began; prior to that date no civil registration of births, deaths, or non-Protestant marriages existed at any level

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Non-Catholic marriages:** Registered from 1 April 1845 by civil superintendent registrars. Presbyterian marriages in County Antrim thus entered the civil record 19 years before all-event registration began.
- **Births, deaths, and Catholic marriages:** Civil registration for all events began 1 January 1864, administered by the General Register Office (GRO) for Ireland; since 1922 the GRO Northern Ireland in Belfast holds registers for what is now Northern Ireland.
- **What exists for 1780–1870:** Only non-Catholic marriages 1845–1870 and all births/deaths/marriages from 1 January 1864 are in the civil record. All earlier vital events are church records only.
- **Where held:** GRO Northern Ireland, Oxford House, 49-55 Chichester Street, Belfast BT1 4HL. Indexes and many original registers are searchable free at IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie).
- **Gaps:** Civil registration covers only the last six years of your target window for births and deaths; the great majority of events 1780–1863 are undocumented in any civil record.

### Church records

This is the central source class for Billy parish in 1780–1870.

**Presbyterian — the priority source for your family**

The Bushmills/Billy area falls within the **Route Presbytery** of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland. The congregation(s) most likely to hold registers for a family living in Billy civil parish are:

- **Bushmills Presbyterian Church** (Route Presbytery) — the congregation seated in the principal town of the civil parish
- **Dervock Presbyterian Church** (a few miles south, also Route Presbytery) — served parts of the surrounding rural area
- **Ballybogy and Kilraghts** presbyterian congregations in the wider Route district may also be relevant depending on exact townland

Important: *Which congregation a household actually used cannot be confirmed from this survey because the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Irish church records were unreachable (see quirks). Verify the congregation(s) covering each townland in Billy parish directly with the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland before searching registers.*

The registers of these congregations — typically recording baptisms and sometimes marriages, rarely burials — are held in two places:
- **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland**, Church House, Fisherwick Place, Belfast BT1 6DW (original registers and deposit copies)
- **PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland)**, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ — holds microfilm copies of many Presbyterian registers; its eCatalogue is searchable at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni

Many FamilySearch microfilm copies of County Antrim Presbyterian registers also exist; this survey could not retrieve collection IDs or coverage dates from FamilySearch because volume_search and collections_search require a resolved standard place name, which was not returned by the tools.

**Church of Ireland (Anglican)**

The Church of Ireland parish of Billy is co-extensive with the civil parish. Its registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the established-church record series. Original registers are held at PRONI; some may also be held by the Representative Church Body Library (RCB Library), Braemor Park, Dublin D14 V796. The Church of Ireland registers for County Antrim parishes are described in the PRONI eCatalogue and many are available on IrishGenealogy.ie.

**Roman Catholic**

The Catholic parish covering Billy civil parish is part of the Diocese of Down and Connor. Catholic registers for this area begin later than Presbyterian or Church of Ireland registers — typically 1820s to 1840s is the earliest for many north Antrim Catholic parishes. Registers are held by the parish (contact the Diocese of Down and Connor) with microfilm copies at the National Library of Ireland, Dublin, and many indexed on IrishGenealogy.ie and Ancestry.

**Methodist**

A small Methodist presence existed in north Antrim; circuit registers are held at the Methodist Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast, and some have been microfilmed by PRONI.

- **Language:** All registers in this area are in English.
- **Gaps:** The 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin destroyed many records (see Known Record Losses below). Presbyterian registers for some congregations begin only in the 1820s or later; check PRONI's eCatalogue for the specific start date of each register before concluding a year has no coverage.

### Census records

- **Irish census records for 1780–1870 are almost entirely lost** — the most significant research challenge in Irish genealogy:
  - 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 returns: largely destroyed in the 1922 PRO Dublin fire; fragments survive for some counties
  - 1861 and 1871 returns: deliberately destroyed by government order after statistical use
  - 1881 and 1891 returns: pulped during World War II
  - **1901 and 1911 returns:** survive complete and are freely searchable at census.nationalarchives.ie — outside your 1780–1870 target but essential for identifying family members still alive
- **Census substitutes for 1780–1870 — these are your primary population-level sources:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837:** Survey of occupiers of tithable land; County Antrim volumes are online at titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie and on Ancestry/FamilySearch. Billy parish is covered.
  - **Griffith's Primary Valuation c. 1858–1864:** Lists all occupiers of property; County Antrim coverage is online free at AskAboutIreland.ie and Griffith's Valuation Online (www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation). This is the most detailed mid-century census substitute.
  - **1831 Census fragments:** The National Archives of Ireland holds fragments for some parishes; check whether Billy parish survived.
  - **1876 Return of Owners of Land:** Published parliamentary paper listing landowners.

### Probate and court records

- **Before 1858:** Probate was proved in the ecclesiastical Consistorial Court of Connor, which had jurisdiction over County Antrim. These records were held in Dublin and largely destroyed in the 1922 fire (see Known Record Losses). The Inland Revenue Betham Abstracts (at the National Archives of Ireland) provide partial pre-1858 coverage — they name testators, executors, and legatees.
- **From 1858:** Probate transferred to the Principal Registry, Dublin, and district registries. County Antrim estates generally went to the **Belfast District Probate Registry**. Annual calendars of grants (indexes) from 1858 survive and are online at the National Archives of Ireland search tool. Original wills proved 1858–1900 were largely destroyed in 1922; the calendars name the deceased, their address, occupation, estate value, and executor.
- **Quarter Sessions and Assizes:** County Antrim court records are at PRONI.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds, with townland as the basic unit; County Antrim land was largely private (plantation-era grants), not public-land-state.
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of deeds, mortgages, and leases registered voluntarily; a County Antrim landowning or leasing family may appear. Index volumes are at the Registry of Deeds, Henrietta Street, Dublin; transcripts and indexes are on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837:** See Census substitutes above — also a land record.
- **Griffith's Valuation c. 1858–1864:** See Census substitutes above — also the foundational land record for the period.
- **Estate papers:** Much of north Antrim was held by a small number of landed estates; estate papers (rent rolls, tenancy agreements, eviction records) are at PRONI and are an underused source for tenant families. The PRONI eCatalogue lists estate papers by parish and townland.
- **Encumbered Estates Court records (post-1849):** Where estates were sold following the Famine, records may name tenants.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** 1798 Rebellion (United Irishmen), Napoleonic Wars 1803–1815, Crimean War 1854–1856
- **British Army service records:** At The National Archives, Kew (series WO). Many pre-1872 records were destroyed in a 1931 fire; surviving records are on Findmypast and Ancestry.
- **Militia and yeomanry:** County Antrim Militia records; some at PRONI.
- **Pension records:** Chelsea pensioner records at The National Archives, Kew, and on Findmypast.
- **Muster rolls:** The National Archives, Kew.

### Cemetery records

- **Principal Church of Ireland burial ground:** Billy (Derrykeighan) or the churchyard at Dunluce, north Antrim — gravestone inscriptions are the most accessible burial record for this period.
- **Online coverage:** Many north Antrim gravestone inscriptions have been transcribed by local historical societies and are partly on Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves (billiongraves.com). The Ulster Historical Foundation has published gravestone surveys.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by the parish. PRONI holds some gravestone transcripts.
- **Presbyterian burial grounds:** Each congregation may have its own graveyard; some are recorded in PRONI and in the Irish Genealogical Research Society's publications.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Coleraine Chronicle* (from 1844) and *Northern Constitution* (from 1876) covered the north Antrim area including Bushmills. The *Belfast Newsletter* (from 1737) is the major regional paper and carried notices of births, marriages, and deaths for County Antrim throughout this period.
- **Where held:** British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) holds digitized runs of many Ulster papers. The *Belfast Newsletter* is online at britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk and the Newspapers.com network. PRONI holds physical microfilm.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices appear; in rural north Antrim coverage is sparser than in Belfast but increases toward the 1860s.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Ulster emigration context:** North Antrim was a major emigration source throughout this period — to North America during the 1780s–1800s, to Canada (especially New Brunswick and Ontario) in the 1820s–1840s, and intensifying during and after the Famine. A family in Billy parish in 1825 may have relatives on both sides of the Atlantic.
- **Relevant ports:** Emigrants left primarily through **Londonderry/Derry** (the main Ulster emigration port), **Belfast**, and occasionally through Scottish ports (Glasgow, Greenock). Some travelled to Liverpool first.
- **Passenger lists:** Pre-1820 lists are sparse; post-1820 US lists are at Ancestry and FamilySearch. Canadian lists are at Library and Archives Canada (bac-lac.gc.ca). The National Archives of Ireland emigration database covers some periods.
- **Naturalization:** US naturalizations for immigrant ancestors are at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch; they often name the port and approximate arrival date.
- **Ulster emigration databases:** The Ulster Historical Foundation's Ulster Covenant/emigrant databases and the PRONI emigration records should be checked.

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1663, 1669):** Earlier than your window but establish a family's presence.
- **Flaxseed Premium List (1796):** Lists of County Antrim linen weavers who received free flaxseed — a significant source for the rural Protestant community, directly applicable to your period's immediate predecessor generation.
- **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837:** Primary substitute for a mid-period census. County Antrim volumes are online.
- **Griffith's Valuation c. 1858–1864:** Effectively a tax-and-land record combined.
- **Poor Law rate books:** From 1838; held at PRONI; list all ratable occupiers and can fill the census gap.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law Union records (from 1838):** Billy civil parish falls within the **Ballymoney Poor Law Union** (and possibly partly Coleraine Union depending on townland). Board of Guardian minute books, relief registers, and workhouse records are at PRONI. For a Famine-period family, these are essential.
- **School records:** National school registers from the 1830s onward; at the National Archives of Ireland (many) and PRONI. Children's ages and sometimes parents' occupations are recorded.
- **Estate and rentals:** See Land records above. Particularly important for Billy parish given the dominance of large estates in north Antrim.
- **Grand Jury presentments:** County Antrim road and infrastructure records; can name local contractors and labourers.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant to this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil registration 1845/1864+; Church of Ireland and Catholic registers; some Presbyterian | No civil record 1780–1864; browse church registers | Free (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) |
| AskAboutIreland.ie | Griffith's Primary Valuation, County Antrim | Census gap 1848–1864 | Free (https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation) |
| National Archives of Ireland | Census fragments, probate calendars 1858+, school records, Tithe Applotment | 1922 fire losses; pre-1864 vital records | Free (https://www.nationalarchives.ie) |
| Tithe Applotment Books | County Antrim 1823–1837 | Census gap pre-1841 | Free (https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) |
| PRONI eCatalogue | Church, land, estate, court records for County Antrim | Physical records not digitized — identifies what exists | Free (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) |
| British Newspaper Archive | *Coleraine Chronicle*, *Belfast Newsletter*, other Ulster papers | Death/marriage notices; no other source | Subscription (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) |
| Findmypast | Irish records, British Army records | Military service and pension records | Subscription (https://www.findmypast.com) |
| Ancestry | Irish records, Registry of Deeds, passenger lists | Multiple gaps | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com) |

**Note:** This survey could not retrieve FamilySearch collection IDs, record counts, or digitization percentages for County Antrim because the place_search tool returned no results for Irish places and the wiki-query-api returned only generic content (see quirks). Check FamilySearch's catalog directly for County Antrim, Ireland, collections: https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| PRONI, Belfast | Church registers (original and microfilm), estate papers, court records, Poor Law records, land records for County Antrim | In-person; some records available via PRONI online service |
| Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast | Original and deposit copies of Presbyterian congregational registers, Route Presbytery records | In-person by appointment |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person by appointment |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Census fragments, probate calendars, school records, state papers | In-person; many indexes online |
| National Library of Ireland, Dublin | Catholic registers (microfilm), Griffith's notebooks, newspapers | In-person; microfilm registers online |
| The National Archives, Kew | British Army service, pension, militia records | In-person; many records on Findmypast/Ancestry |
| GRO Northern Ireland, Belfast | Civil registration registers from 1845/1864 | In-person; indexes and many images at IrishGenealogy.ie |

## Records NOT online

- **PRONI-held original church registers** not yet digitized: Many Presbyterian and Church of Ireland registers are microfilmed at PRONI but not yet fully online. PRONI's eCatalogue identifies what exists; physical or microfilm access is required.
- **Estate papers and rentals:** Almost entirely physical at PRONI; not digitized beyond the PRONI eCatalogue finding aid.
- **Poor Law rate books and Board of Guardian minutes:** At PRONI; physical access only.
- **Grand Jury presentments:** Physical at PRONI.
- **Most pre-1858 wills and administration bonds** (see Known Record Losses below).

## Known record losses

- **1922 Public Record Office fire, Dublin (30 June 1922):** The Four Courts building was destroyed during the Irish Civil War. This fire consumed:
  - Census returns for 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 (mostly; some county fragments survive)
  - Most wills and administration bonds proved in ecclesiastical courts before 1858
  - Many Church of Ireland parish registers (those deposited in Dublin)
  - Numerous other record classes
  - County Antrim Church of Ireland registers that had been deposited in Dublin were lost; those retained locally (now at PRONI or the RCB Library) survived. Presbyterian registers were generally held locally and were not destroyed.
- **Destruction of 1861 and 1871 census returns:** Ordered destroyed by the government after statistical extraction; no names survive.
- **1931 War Office fire, Middlesex:** Destroyed a large proportion of British Army service records for other ranks serving before 1920.
- Substitute sources for lost wills: Inland Revenue Betham Abstracts, the annual probate calendars from 1858, and testamentary entries in the Registry of Deeds.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation** before searching any other record class. Together they bracket the key pre-census period and place your family in a specific townland, which then focuses every subsequent search. The townland is the unit that connects church registers, estate records, and Poor Law records.
- **Identify the specific townland in Billy parish.** The civil parish contains multiple townlands; church register coverage, estate ownership, and Poor Law union membership can differ between adjacent townlands. The Griffith's Valuation and Tithe Books will establish the townland.
- **For a Presbyterian family, the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland** is the essential first contact for church registers. The Route Presbytery covers the Bushmills area; write or visit to establish which congregation's registers cover the specific townland and what dates they begin. Registers sometimes begin later than the founding of the congregation.
- **Search the Flaxseed Premium List of 1796.** County Antrim is extensively covered; for a linen-weaving Presbyterian family in the Route area it may name the grandparents' generation and establish the family in a specific townland a generation before Griffith's.
- **Poor Law records 1838–1870** (Ballymoney Union) are an underused source that fills much of the gap between Griffith's and the 1901 census. Rate books name every ratable household annually.
- **Cross the boundary into County Londonderry/Derry.** The north Antrim coast is close to the Coleraine area of County Londonderry; a family in the western townlands of Billy parish may have used Coleraine-area churches, registered in Coleraine district, and had relatives on both sides of the county line. Search Coleraine Poor Law Union and Coleraine parish registers in parallel.

**FamilySearch Wiki unreachable during this survey (Ireland Genealogy, Ireland Vital Records, County Antrim Genealogy, Ireland Church Records, Ireland Census, Ireland Land and Property, Ireland Probate Records, Northern Ireland Genealogy pages); these pages may exist — re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence. The place_search tool also returned no results for Irish places, preventing collections_search, volume_search, and external_links_search from running. FamilySearch collection IDs, record counts, and digitization levels for County Antrim could not be verified in this survey.**

---

This guide covers Billy civil parish (Bushmills area), County Antrim, Ireland, for 1780–1870, a period that falls almost entirely before civil vital registration began. For a Presbyterian family the essential sources are the Route Presbytery congregation registers (held at PRONI and the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland in Belfast), the 1796 Flaxseed Premium List, the 1823–1837 Tithe Applotment Books, and Griffith's Primary Valuation of about 1858–1864 — these together can carry a family back through most of the target period, compensating for the near-total loss of Irish census records. The two warnings that matter most are the 1922 Public Record Office fire (which destroyed most pre-1858 wills and many Church of Ireland registers) and the absence of civil birth and death registration before January 1864, meaning every pre-1864 vital event is in a church register that may or may not survive.

The next step is to identify the specific townland in Billy parish from Griffith's Valuation or the Tithe Books, then contact the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland to confirm which Route Presbytery congregation served that townland and the start date of its surviving registers — that pins down the primary source before any other search begins.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
County Cork, established as a county from 1606, is in the Province of Munster, with Cork City as its administrative center. The county's population in the 1830s–1840s was predominantly Irish Catholic, with a Protestant (Church of Ireland) minority. Key context: the Great Famine began in 1845, overlapping the end of your target window, and massive emigration through Cobh (then Queenstown) generated significant emigration records.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Critical gap:** State registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did **not begin until 1 January 1864**. Non-Catholic (Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from **1845** onward.
- **For 1830s–1840s Catholic families:** No civil certificates exist. Church records are the essential substitute.

### Church Records
- **Roman Catholic registers** (baptisms and marriages) are the primary source for the 1830s–1840s. Available free online through the National Library of Ireland (registers.nli.ie). Many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, though survival varies by parish.
- **Church of Ireland registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) held at the Representative Church Body Library, Dublin.
- **Language note:** Many Roman Catholic registers use Latin for sacramental entries.

### Census Records — Major Losses
- The 1841 and 1851 census returns were almost entirely **destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire**. The 1861 and 1871 returns were destroyed by government order. The first surviving national census is **1901**.
- **Census substitutes (critical):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists land occupiers by townland — the principal census substitute for the 1830s. Available digitized online via FamilySearch.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s for Cork):** Lists every householder with their property and landlord. The major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses. Indexed and free online.

### Probate and Court Records
- The **1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the great majority of pre-1900 Irish wills and administrations**. This is a critical loss for 1830s–1840s ancestors.
- **Surviving substitutes:** Will abstracts and indexes compiled before the fire survive at the National Archives of Ireland.
- Jurisdiction ran through the Consistorial Court of Cork and Ross before 1858.

### Land Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** and **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s)** are the core land records (see Census substitutes above).
- **Estate records:** Many Cork families were tenants on landed estates; rent rolls and tenant lists may survive in the National Archives of Ireland and National Library of Ireland.
- **Important:** Ireland had a landlord-tenant system — deeds of sale for ordinary tenant farmers are uncommon.

### Immigration/Emigration Records
- **Cobh (Queenstown)** was the primary emigration port for County Cork. Famine-era (1845–1852) passenger manifests are especially rich.
- **Important:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — search the full manifest, not just the head of household.
- Arrival manifests for the US are held at NARA (online via Ancestry and FamilySearch); Canadian arrivals at Library and Archives Canada.

### Military Records
- For Irish men in British Army service: service records (muster rolls, discharge papers, pension records) held at The National Archives, Kew, UK.

### Cemetery Records
- Many rural Catholic churchyards have no surviving formal burial register for the 1830s–1840s. Church of Ireland burial registers, where surviving, are at the Representative Church Body Library.
- Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers many Cork cemeteries.

### Newspapers
- Cork had active newspapers in the 1830s–1840s, including the **Cork Examiner** (founded 1841). Holdings at the British Library Newspaper Archive and National Library of Ireland; also Newspapers.com.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (registers.nli.ie) | Roman Catholic parish registers to 1880 | Free online |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Tithe Applotment Books; will abstracts; estate papers | In-person; some online |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Tithe Applotment Books; Griffith's Valuation; indexed Irish records | Free |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland parish registers | In-person; some via FamilySearch |
| Cork City and County Archives | Local government and estate records | In-person |
| NARA (archives.gov) | US arrival passenger manifests | Free; also Ancestry |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Cork | Free |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with church records, not civil registration.** For Catholic families in the 1830s–1840s, Roman Catholic parish registers — accessed free through the National Library of Ireland — are the first documentary source.

2. **Identify the townland first.** Catholic parish registers are filed by parish (which are townland-based), not by county. Use the Tithe Applotment Books to place your ancestor in a specific townland, then identify the corresponding parish.

3. **Follow up with Griffith's Valuation.** Even if your ancestor emigrated in the 1840s, other family members who remained can confirm the household location.

4. **Search the full passenger manifest.** Famine-era lists from Cobh/Queenstown record every family member including infants — don't search only for the head of household.

5. **Expect significant record losses.** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed nearly all 1841/1851 census returns and most pre-1858 wills. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation survive as the main substitutes.

6. **A negative online search result doesn't mean no record exists.** Many Cork church registers survive but are not indexed — they can only be browsed image by image. Without knowing the townland and parish, you cannot identify the right register to browse.

---

County Cork in the 1830s–1840s sits in one of the most record-scarce windows in Irish genealogy: civil registration hadn't begun, census returns were later destroyed, and most wills were lost in 1922. The surviving core sources are **Roman Catholic parish registers** (NLI, free online), the **Tithe Applotment Books** for the 1820s–1830s, and **Griffith's Valuation** for the early 1850s — these three together can often place a family in a specific townland and document baptisms and marriages. Once your ancestor emigrated through Cobh, search the full passenger manifest for every family member.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** County Cork was established as a county from 1606, as recorded in the place data returned for this survey.
- **Administrative center:** Cork City (the county town)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Munster, Ireland
- **Population during period:** The population tool returned no data for this place and period — figures are not available from this survey's tool results.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural, with significant maritime trade through Cork Harbour (Cobh/Queenstown); farming families generated tithe and valuation land records, the core substitutes for this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly Irish Catholic, with a Protestant (Church of Ireland) minority, particularly among landowners and urban merchants — which denomination your ancestor belonged to determines which church records to consult.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the large majority); Church of Ireland (Anglican); Presbyterian and Methodist congregations present in Cork City and some towns.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine began in 1845, overlapping the end of your target window; the period also saw Daniel O'Connell's Catholic Emancipation movement (1829) and widespread tenant unrest — Famine-era emigration through Cobh/Queenstown was massive and generated emigration records.

## Boundary changes
- County Cork's boundaries were stable during the target period (1830s–1840s).
- The county falls entirely within the Province of Munster for all jurisdictional purposes.
- **No pre-formation split applies** — the county existed well before the 1830s.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** State registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did not begin until **1 January 1864** (statewide level). Non-Catholic (primarily Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from **1845** at the state level. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **What exists for 1830s–1840s:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates. The civil registration system simply did not exist for Catholic families in this window. Church of Ireland marriages have civil registration only from 1845 onward.
- **Where held:** When they begin (1864 onward), civil records are held by the General Register Office, Ireland, with indexes online at IrishGenealogy.ie.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1830s–1840s window is a gap for civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Roman Catholic parish registers are the essential substitute — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic parishes cover virtually the entire county; Church of Ireland parishes are present throughout; Presbyterian and Methodist congregations exist in Cork City.
- **Record types:** Roman Catholic registers record baptisms and marriages (burials are rarely recorded). Church of Ireland registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **Where held:** The National Library of Ireland holds microfilm and digital images of Roman Catholic registers up to 1880, available free online. Church of Ireland registers are held by the Representative Church Body Library (Dublin) and sometimes in local custody. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Survival:** Survival varies widely by parish; the wiki page notes that many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s, so some registers reach back into your target window, while others do not start until later or were lost.
- **Gaps:** No tool result returned a list of surviving Cork Catholic parishes by start date — consult the National Library of Ireland's online catalogue (registers.nli.ie) directly to check whether your specific parish's registers survive and when they begin. The 1922 Four Courts fire did not affect most church registers, which were held separately.
- **Language:** Latin is used in many Roman Catholic registers for sacramental entries; Church of Ireland registers are in English.

### Census records
- **National census:** The first usable Irish national census was 1841. The 1841 and 1851 census returns were almost entirely destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. The 1861 and 1871 returns were destroyed by government order. The first surviving national census is **1901**. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Census substitutes (critical for this period):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** List occupiers of tithe-liable land across Ireland, including County Cork. These are the principal census substitute for the 1830s. They record the occupier's name, townland, and acreage. Available in digitized form online.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork in the early 1850s):** Lists every householder, with the property they occupied and the landowner above them. It is the major substitute for the destroyed 1841 and 1851 censuses for County Cork. Available indexed and free online (Ask About Ireland / Griffith's Valuation online).
- **Other enumerations:** This survey did not confirm any additional state or ecclesiastical census for this period beyond those above.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, grants of administration, inventories.
- **Record loss:** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the great majority of pre-1900 Irish wills and administrations held at the Principal Registry, Dublin. This is a critical loss for 1830s–1840s Cork ancestors. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Surviving substitutes:** Will abstracts and indexes compiled before the fire survive at the National Archives of Ireland and the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI). Published will calendars (indexes) for the Prerogative Court of Armagh and the Consistorial Court of Cork and Ross may survive for some individuals.
- **Date range:** Probate jurisdiction for County Cork ran through the Consistorial Court of Cork and Ross before 1858, then through the district probate registries.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland, Dublin; some abstracts at the Royal Irish Academy. The specific holding repository for originals that survived should be confirmed through the National Archives of Ireland directly — this survey's tools did not return details beyond the general record-loss note.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Ireland used a townland-based system (not the rectangular township survey of the United States). The Ordnance Survey townland maps (1830s–1840s, covering Cork) are a critical finding tool.
- **Key record sets:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** See Census records above — also serve as land occupancy records.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s for Cork):** See Census records above.
  - **Estate records:** Many Cork families were tenants on landed estates; estate papers (rent rolls, eviction notices, tenant lists) survive in the National Archives of Ireland and the National Library of Ireland, though access varies by estate.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland; National Library of Ireland; online via Ask About Ireland and other digitization projects.
- **Land distribution:** Ireland had a landlord-tenant system, not a land-grant system; deeds of sale or lease for tenant farmers are uncommon. The land distribution jurisdiction was the landed estate, not a government land office.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The British Army was the relevant military service for Irish men in the 1830s–1840s. No major conflict in Ireland itself, but service in India and other British Empire postings was common.
- **Record types:** Army service records (muster rolls, description books, discharge papers), pension records.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (Kew, UK) holds British Army service records. This survey's tool results did not return a dedicated Ireland military records page — the FamilySearch Wiki pages requested for this topic all resolved to the generic Ireland Genealogy page and did not provide further detail.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic and Church of Ireland graveyards present throughout County Cork; large urban cemeteries include St. Finbarr's Cemetery, Cork City.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers many Cork cemeteries; the tool returned this URL as a curated external link.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary; many rural Catholic churchyards have no surviving formal burial register for the 1830s–1840s. Church of Ireland burial registers, where they survive, are at the Representative Church Body Library.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Cork had active newspapers in the 1830s–1840s, including the Cork Examiner (founded 1841) and earlier titles. This survey did not return specific newspaper holdings via the tool results.
- **Where held:** The British Library Newspaper Archive and the National Library of Ireland hold Irish newspaper collections; Newspapers.com was returned as a curated external link by the tool.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale announcements, and legal notices (land evictions, court proceedings) are valuable for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Cobh (then called Queenstown) was the primary emigration port for County Cork; Cork City's quays also handled departures.
- **Record types:** Passenger departure lists; arrival manifests at American, Canadian, and Australian ports. Famine-era (1845–1852) passenger manifests are the richest source, extending just past the target window.
- **Important note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching an emigrating family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Where held:** Arrival manifests for the United States are held at NARA (online via Ancestry and FamilySearch); Canadian arrivals at Library and Archives Canada; Australian arrivals at state archives. Irish departure records for this period are sparse.

- **Types:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) are both a land record and the closest thing to a tax roll for this period. County Cess (local tax) records may survive in some parishes but were not confirmed by this survey's tool results.

---

## Records NOT online

- **Church of Ireland parish registers** for many Cork parishes: held at the Representative Church Body Library; not all are digitized or indexed online.
- **Estate papers and rent rolls:** Mostly physical at the National Archives of Ireland and National Library of Ireland; not systematically digitized.
- **County Cess and local tax records:** Not confirmed as online for this period.
- **Surviving probate abstracts:** Some at the National Archives of Ireland; not fully online.
- **British Army service records for Irish soldiers:** Held at The National Archives, Kew (UK); some accessible online via Ancestry (subscription), but many are physical only.

---

## Known record losses

- **1922 Four Courts fire:** This tool-confirmed loss destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns (including the 1841 and 1851 censuses for Cork), and the great majority of original pre-1858 wills and administrations held at the Principal Registry, Dublin. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy). The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation survive as substitutes for census; will abstracts and indexes compiled before the fire survive as partial substitutes for probate.
- **1861 and 1871 census returns:** Destroyed by government order — this survey's tool results do not state the reason, only that they do not survive.
- **Church register losses:** Survival varies by parish. The 1922 fire did not directly affect most church registers (held separately), but individual parish fires and damp have caused local losses. Consult the National Library of Ireland's catalogue to check each specific Cork parish.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with church records, not civil registration.** For 1830s–1840s Cork, there are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for Catholic families. Roman Catholic parish registers — baptisms and marriages — are the first documentary source, accessed free through the National Library of Ireland's registers portal. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Use the Tithe Applotment Books to place your ancestor in a specific townland.** The Books (1823–1837) cover Cork and name land occupiers by townland. Knowing the townland is essential to identifying which Catholic parish to search, since parishes are townland-based, not civil-boundary-based. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Follow up with Griffith's Valuation for the early 1850s.** Even if your ancestor emigrated in the 1840s, other family members may remain and can confirm the household location. The Valuation covers all of Cork and is indexed by name. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Search the full passenger manifest for the emigrating family.** Famine-era passenger lists from Cobh/Queenstown record infants and children alongside parents — do not search only for the head of household. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Do not assume a negative online result means no record exists.** Many Cork church registers survive but are not indexed — only browsable image by image. The National Library of Ireland's registers portal requires knowing the parish; without a townland, you cannot identify the right parish to browse.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for specific Ireland topics** (land records, probate, census, church records, naming customs) all resolved to the same generic Ireland Genealogy page during this survey — the topic-specific pages were not reachable. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki for any of these topics for more detail than this guide provides.

---

County Cork in the 1830s and 1840s sits in one of the most record-scarce windows in Irish genealogy: civil registration had not yet begun, nearly all census returns were later destroyed, and most wills were lost in 1922. The surviving core sources are Roman Catholic parish registers (held free online by the National Library of Ireland), the Tithe Applotment Books for the 1820s–1830s, and Griffith's Valuation for the early 1850s — these three together can often place a family in a specific townland and document baptisms and marriages. The most important warning is that you must identify the specific townland your ancestor lived in before you can find the right Catholic parish register, because registers are filed by parish rather than by county. Once your ancestor emigrated through Cobh, search the full passenger manifest for every family member — even infants are listed.

# Locality Guide: Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, Slovenia (c. 1812)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Historical name:** Bischoflack, Krain (Carniola), Austria — the FamilySearch Catalog records this area under "Bischoflack (Krain)"
- **Modern municipality:** Škofja Loka, Slovenia
- **Religious affiliation:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Ljubljana)

---

## The Short Answer

For an 1812 marriage, search the **Roman Catholic parish marriage register** for whichever parish served Javorje. Those registers were kept in Latin, following a tabular format adopted in 1770/1784 under Emperor Joseph II.

**Important caveat:** The specific parish that covered Javorje nad Škofjo Loko in 1812 is not confirmed by this survey — identifying the serving parish is the essential first step.

---

## Where to Look

### 1. Matricula Online *(start here)*
- **URL:** https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/
- Hosts images of Slovenia Catholic church records; this is the primary online source for Slovenian parish registers
- Search there for the relevant parish's marriage register once the parish is identified

### 2. FamilySearch Catalog
- Search under "Škofja Loka" or the historical name "Bischoflack, Krain, Austria"
- 36 catalog items exist for this area; two items are confirmed online:
  - *Kirchliche Angelegenheiten 1550–1747* (koha:422727, film 1416653) — church documents for the area
  - *Knjiga hiš v Škofji Loki* by France Štukl (koha:502892, film 1183591) — a compiled book of houses and inhabitants; FamilySearch Library only, not online
- **Note:** The FamilySearch volume search returned **0 digitized volumes** for Škofja Loka for 1790–1830, confirming the parish registers are not in FamilySearch's main image database for this period

### 3. Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana *(for originals or parish identification)*
- **Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana**
- Krekov trg 1, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia
- Email: arhiv.lj@rkc.si
- Holds original pre-1880s parish registers for the Archdiocese of Ljubljana

---

## Key Facts for 1812

- **Civil registration did not yet exist** — only the Catholic parish register records this marriage; no civil marriage record exists for this date
- **No duplicate registers in 1812** — civil duplicate registers were not mandated until 1835 (Catholic) and 1829 (Evangelical), so only the parish's own copy of the marriage entry exists
- **Record language:** Latin
- **Status animarum** (household lists of parishioners, extant from 1750) can supplement the marriage register if the entry is hard to find

---

## Record Losses

No tool result reports destruction or loss of parish registers for the Škofja Loka area. The absence of digitized volumes in FamilySearch for this date range is a **coverage gap**, not a confirmed loss.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Contact the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana** (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to identify which parish served Javorje c. 1812
2. **Search that parish's marriage register on Matricula Online** (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/)
3. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog** directly for additional holdings under "Škofja Loka" and "Bischoflack"

## Research tips
- **Start with Matricula Online** (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/): the FamilySearch Slovenia Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Slovenia_Church_Records) names this as the online home for Slovenia church record images; it is the first place to look for the 1812 marriage register
- **Identify the serving parish before searching:** The specific parish that covered Javorje in 1812 is not confirmed by any tool result; contacting the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to establish the parish assignment is a necessary first step before ordering records
- **Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly** for the remaining 32 items filed under Škofja Loka (https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) — the catalog found 36 total items but this survey only detailed 4
- **Records are in Latin:** Marriage entries in Catholic parish registers from 1812 follow the tabular format introduced in 1770/1784; the researcher must be able to read Latin or obtain a translation
- **Status animarum as a supplement:** If the marriage register entry is hard to locate, the status animarum (household list of parishioners, extant from 1750) may confirm the family's presence and date range in the parish (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Slovenia_Church_Records)
- **Duplicate registers were not yet required in 1812:** Civil duplicate registers were mandated only in 1835 (Catholic) and 1829 (Evangelical), so only the parish's own copy of the marriage entry exists for 1812 — the archdiocesan archive is the definitive repository

---

For an 1812 marriage in Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, the record would have been made in the Catholic parish marriage register for whichever parish served that small village in Carniola. Those pre-1880 original registers are held at the Archdiocese of Ljubljana's archive in Ljubljana (Nadškofijski arhiv, email: arhiv.lj@rkc.si), and images of Slovenian Catholic church records are available to browse online at Matricula Online (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/). The most important warning is that this survey could not confirm which specific parish covered Javorje in 1812 — establishing that parish assignment by contacting the archive directly is the essential first step before searching any register.

The next step is to contact the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana to identify the serving parish for Javorje c. 1812, then search that parish's marriage register on Matricula Online.
