entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700–1800, Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally settled as New Amsterdam (Dutch colony) in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York; city within New York Province (British colonial)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County and capital of New York Province
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colonial) until 1783; thereafter New York State
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by this survey's tools
- **Economy:** Major commercial Atlantic port and colonial administrative center
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, and other European settlers; enslaved African population; small Jewish community (Congregation Shearith Israel)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, Jewish; smaller Baptist and Quaker communities
- **Key historical events:** British seizure from Dutch 1664; Revolutionary War British occupation 1776–1783; American independence 1783

## Boundary changes
- **1664:** Dutch colonial jurisdiction (New Netherland) replaced by British New York Province; administrative records shifted from Dutch to English systems, though Dutch church records continued independently
- For the 1700s, research centers on Manhattan (New York County); the five modern boroughs were not consolidated until 1898
- After 1783, provincial-era record series ended and New York State systems began; records bridging this transition may fall in either the colonial or early-state series

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in colonial New York; the FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to New York vital registration dates did not return specific information during this survey
- **What exists:** Church records — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the sole source for vital events throughout the colonial period
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch collections; see Church records below
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil registration for births, marriages, or deaths during the 1700s
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate records for death and heirs

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (continuous registers from 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, Manhattan), Presbyterian, Lutheran, Jewish (Shearith Israel)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062, 2,345,678 records) covers the colonial period; one digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007733180) covers Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700–1776, 211 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), in Dutch; the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and New-York Historical Society hold extensive church record holdings per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Gaps:** Anglican, Presbyterian, and Lutheran colonial registers are not broken out as separate digitized volumes in this survey's results; their online status is unconfirmed here
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch; a reader of Dutch is required to use the browse-only FamilySearch volume

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — after the colonial period; no federal enumeration exists for the 1700s
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial tax assessment lists and militia rolls serve as population substitutes; the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)) states that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards, and that colonial militia rolls list men of military age
- **Access:** No indexed online census for the colonial period

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories; wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York
- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection 1542780, 987,654 records) covers the colonial period
- **Court records:** Mayor's Court records are named in the FamilySearch Wiki as a key source; New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives hold administrative and court records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial period)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Grants and patents were issued under the authority of the New York Governor and Crown; the specific office holding original patents is not confirmed by this survey's tools — consult the New York State Archives
- **Types:** Land conveyances, deeds, patents; FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection 2078654, 1,567,890 records)
- **Date range:** From 1630
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection above; originals at New York State Archives and New York County Clerk

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (from FamilySearch Wiki); Revolutionary War service records and pension files
- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls at the New York State Archives; Revolutionary War records at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church (Manhattan) and other congregational burial grounds; colonial-era gravestones survive at several Manhattan churchyards
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some colonial-era headstones
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual churches

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette is noted in Wikipedia as operating during the colonial period
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and library microfilm
- **Content value:** Death notices, legal notices, and land transaction announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was a major Atlantic port throughout the colonial period
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; colonial-era lists may be fragmentary
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry.com for digitized passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists (ward-level for some years); FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection 1678432, 123,456 records) — this begins at 1799, partly outside the colonial period
- **Date range:** Some lists survive from earlier in the 1700s; the FamilySearch Wiki names them without giving specific year ranges
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection above; earlier lists at New York State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household and are the primary substitute for census-type information before 1790

### Other record types
- **Colonial Manuscripts:** New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives document provincial administration and court proceedings (from FamilySearch Wiki)
- **Jewish community records:** Congregation Shearith Israel (oldest Jewish congregation in North America) maintained its own vital and community records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640–1940 (collection 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (collection 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (collection 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804 (collection 1678432); 1 browse-only Dutch Reformed volume 1700–1776 (image group 007733180) | Vital events (via church), land, probate, tax | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger lists and digitized collections | Immigration, supplemental records | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records | Revolutionary War service and pension | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Burial information, colonial-era gravestones | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Death notices, legal notices, land transactions | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| NARA | Federal holdings | Passenger lists, Revolutionary War records | Free / in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches New York City and the period 1700–1800; this is the complete result returned by the survey (totalResults: 1).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court records; land patents; militia rolls | In-person / online finding aids |

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700–1800, Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally settled as New Amsterdam (Dutch colony) in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York; city within New York Province (British colonial)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County and capital of New York Province
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colonial) until 1783; thereafter New York State
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by this survey's tools
- **Economy:** Major commercial Atlantic port and colonial administrative center
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, and other European settlers; enslaved African population; small Jewish community (Congregation Shearith Israel)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, Jewish; smaller Baptist and Quaker communities
- **Key historical events:** British seizure from Dutch 1664; Revolutionary War British occupation 1776–1783; American independence 1783

## Boundary changes
- **1664:** Dutch colonial jurisdiction (New Netherland) replaced by British New York Province; administrative records shifted from Dutch to English systems, though Dutch church records continued independently
- For the 1700s, research centers on Manhattan (New York County); the five modern boroughs were not consolidated until 1898
- After 1783, provincial-era record series ended and New York State systems began; records bridging this transition may fall in either the colonial or early-state series

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in colonial New York; the FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to New York vital registration dates did not return specific information during this survey
- **What exists:** Church records — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the sole source for vital events throughout the colonial period
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch collections; see Church records below
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil registration for births, marriages, or deaths during the 1700s
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate records for death and heirs

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (continuous registers from 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, Manhattan), Presbyterian, Lutheran, Jewish (Shearith Israel)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062, 2,345,678 records) covers the colonial period; one digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007733180) covers Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700–1776, 211 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), in Dutch; the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and New-York Historical Society hold extensive church record holdings per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Gaps:** Anglican, Presbyterian, and Lutheran colonial registers are not broken out as separate digitized volumes in this survey's results; their online status is unconfirmed here
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch; a reader of Dutch is required to use the browse-only FamilySearch volume

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — after the colonial period; no federal enumeration exists for the 1700s
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial tax assessment lists and militia rolls serve as population substitutes; the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)) states that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards, and that colonial militia rolls list men of military age
- **Access:** No indexed online census for the colonial period

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories; wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York
- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection 1542780, 987,654 records) covers the colonial period
- **Court records:** Mayor's Court records are named in the FamilySearch Wiki as a key source; New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives hold administrative and court records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial period)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Grants and patents were issued under the authority of the New York Governor and Crown; the specific office holding original patents is not confirmed by this survey's tools — consult the New York State Archives
- **Types:** Land conveyances, deeds, patents; FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection 2078654, 1,567,890 records)
- **Date range:** From 1630
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection above; originals at New York State Archives and New York County Clerk

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (from FamilySearch Wiki); Revolutionary War service records and pension files
- **Where held:** Colonial militia rolls at the New York State Archives; Revolutionary War records at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church (Manhattan) and other congregational burial grounds; colonial-era gravestones survive at several Manhattan churchyards
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some colonial-era headstones
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual churches

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette is noted in Wikipedia as operating during the colonial period
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and library microfilm
- **Content value:** Death notices, legal notices, and land transaction announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was a major Atlantic port throughout the colonial period
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; colonial-era lists may be fragmentary
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry.com for digitized passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists (ward-level for some years); FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection 1678432, 123,456 records) — this begins at 1799, partly outside the colonial period
- **Date range:** Some lists survive from earlier in the 1700s; the FamilySearch Wiki names them without giving specific year ranges
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection above; earlier lists at New York State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household and are the primary substitute for census-type information before 1790

### Other record types
- **Colonial Manuscripts:** New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives document provincial administration and court proceedings (from FamilySearch Wiki)
- **Jewish community records:** Congregation Shearith Israel (oldest Jewish congregation in North America) maintained its own vital and community records

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640–1940 (collection 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (collection 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (collection 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804 (collection 1678432); 1 browse-only Dutch Reformed volume 1700–1776 (image group 007733180) | Vital events (via church), land, probate, tax | Free |

| Fold3 | Military records | Revolutionary War service and pension | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Burial information, colonial-era gravestones | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Death notices, legal notices, land transactions | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| NARA | Federal holdings | Passenger lists, Revolutionary War records | Free / in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches New York City and the period 1700–1800; this is the complete result returned by the survey (totalResults: 1).

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| New York State Archives | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court records; land patents; militia rolls | In-person / online finding aids |

| Denominational archives | Dutch Reformed, Presbyterian, Lutheran registers | Contact each denomination separately |

**Virginia, 1775–1783 — Revolutionary War Research Guide**

Virginia in 1775–1783 was one of the best-documented British colonies turned American states, with county-level records reaching back to the 1630s, but the period presents one critical trap: **the 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed**, so the **1782 personal property tax lists** are the essential starting point for placing any household in this era.

**Key sources for Revolutionary War families:**

- **Military pension files** at the National Archives — often name the veteran's wife, children, and ages, making them exceptionally rich genealogically
- **Virginia militia records** at the Library of Virginia in Richmond
- **Bounty land warrant records** connecting veterans to post-war land claims in Ohio
- **FamilySearch** holds five indexed collections covering military, church, land, tax, and court records for this period, plus three digitized image volumes (one browsable but not name-searchable)

**Vital records note:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in Virginia in 1775–1783. **Church vestry registers** — especially Anglican/Episcopal — served that role and are the records to target for vital events.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies, with county-level record-keeping established from the 1630s. It became the Commonwealth of Virginia in 1776. Per Wikipedia, Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony, and the decisive battle of Yorktown (1781) was fought on Virginia soil.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Colony of Virginia until 1776; thereafter an independent Commonwealth
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture, trade; wartime requisitions, privateering
- **Ethnic composition:** British-descended settlers, enslaved African Americans (a large share of the population), Scots-Irish and German settlers in western piedmont and valley regions
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church through 1784), Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Quaker, Lutheran
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Virginia disestablished the Anglican Church in 1784, disrupting parish recordkeeping; wartime disruption affected county record survival

## Boundary changes
- During 1775–1783, Virginia's territory was much larger than today, encompassing what is now West Virginia (not separated until 1863) and the Kentucky District (became the state of Kentucky in 1792). Records for ancestors in those regions were created under Virginia county jurisdiction.
- Virginia county boundaries shifted frequently as western regions were organized into new counties. Always identify the specific county in which your ancestor lived and confirm that county's existence at the relevant date.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia had no statewide civil vital registration during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Vital Records page was not accessible during this survey (returned only generic content); no specific statewide registration start year can be confirmed from this survey's tool results.
- **What exists:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths at state level in this period.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil registration
- **Gaps:** No civil vital records for 1775–1783
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal vestry registers (the official record of baptisms, marriages, and burials through disestablishment); county court marriage bonds and licenses held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (most complete colonial-era records), Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; vestry minutes also recorded poor relief and local administration
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 — Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230); originals at the Library of Virginia and denominational archives
- **Gaps:** Anglican disestablishment (1784) disrupted parish recordkeeping in many Virginia counties; some vestry books were lost during and after the war. Quaker meeting records are typically the most complete among dissenting groups.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — it does not survive. The first extant federal census for Virginia is 1800. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, county tax lists from the 1780s are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State/provincial census:** No Virginia state census is confirmed by this survey's tool results for the 1775–1783 period.
- **Other enumerations:** FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations and tax lists, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, 87 images). This volume is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — it must be searched as text, not browsed name by name.
- **Access:** Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable (not name-indexed). FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850) covers the overlap period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships; county court minute books, order books
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts operated continuously from the colonial period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2134567 — Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). FamilySearch also holds a digitized volume of Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed with images). Originals at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia.
- **Note:** County court minute books name people involved in local administration, road maintenance, poor relief, and petitions — not only formal litigants.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia land patents issued by the colonial/Commonwealth government. Revolutionary War veterans received bounty land warrants redeemable in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their land claims. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages; Revolutionary War land bounty warrants; FamilySearch collection 1734285 — Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285). FamilySearch also holds a digitized volume of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (image group 005301447, 341 images) — browse-only images, not name-indexed, not full-text searchable: must be browsed image by image with no search aid.
- **Date range:** Deeds from county formation; bounty warrants from 1779 onward
- **Where held:** County deed books at county courthouses and Library of Virginia; bounty warrant records at the Library of Virginia and NARA

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls at NARA, Record Group 93 (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia, Richmond (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files at NARA, Record Group 15 (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - Published Virginia State Navy records (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
  - FamilySearch collection 1945678 — Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
- **Where held:** NARA (federal records), Library of Virginia (state militia), FamilySearch (digitized collection), Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/ — subscription required)
- **Note:** Pension files (NARA RG 15) are among the richest sources for Revolutionary War families — they can include the veteran's own service narrative, family composition, ages of members, and residence at the time of application.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Family cemeteries on farms and plantations were common in this period; church graveyards associated with Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Baptist congregations
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Virginia cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Vestry books sometimes recorded burials; sexton records where they survive

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published during the colonial/Revolutionary period — contains military notices, estate notices, and war news
- **Where held:** Historical Newspapers available at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); physical holdings at the Library of Virginia and university libraries
- **Content value:** Militia call-ups, estate administrator notices, deserter notices, loyalist property forfeiture notices, wartime announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Hampton Roads (Norfolk/Hampton), Alexandria
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (from colonial period); for the Revolutionary period, Loyalist emigration to Canada or Britain may be documented in British and Canadian archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax lists (from 1782), land tax lists
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 — Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) begins at 1782; volume 005301449 covers 1782–1799
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1456723; FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable)
- **Substitute value:** Virginia's 1782 personal property tax lists are the standard substitute for the destroyed 1790 federal census and the earliest statewide enumeration of household heads for this period.

### Other record types
- **Loyalist claims:** Virginians who sided with the British had property confiscated; Loyalist Claims Commission records (AO 12 and AO 13) are held at The National Archives, Kew, England — physical access or microfilm
- **Legislative petitions:** Virginia's General Assembly received petitions throughout the war, naming petitioners and those complained against; held at the Library of Virginia

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (1945678); Church Records, 1680–1929 (1598230); Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (1734285); Tax Records, 1782–1850 (1456723); County Court Records, 1650–1920 (2134567) | Multiple record types for the target period | Free |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Revolutionary War service records, pension files — no civil vital records for 1775–1783 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Wartime and postwar burials not in church registers | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Service records (RG 93), pensions (RG 15) | Federal military records | Free / in-person |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Virginia Gazette and wartime papers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 3 digitized volumes match Virginia for 1775–1783; all 3 were examined (the complete result set returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, state archives, land records, legislative petitions, vestry records | In-person; some records online at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | In-person at Washington DC / College Park; Fold3 for digitized holdings |
| County courthouses (various) | Deed books, court minute books, marriage bonds | In-person or mail request |
| The National Archives, Kew, England | Loyalist Claims Commission (AO 12, AO 13) | In-person or document copy request |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized
- Loyalist Claims Commission records (British National Archives, Kew) are physical only
- Virginia General Assembly legislative petitions — many not online
- Many county deed books and court minute books survive only at county courthouses
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume (image group 005301447, 341 images) is browse-only with no name index

## Known record losses
- Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782 personal property tax lists are the standard substitute. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- Empty search results in any other collection are a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction, except for the 1790 census as stated above.

## Research tips
- Begin with the 1782 personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723, volume 005301449) to place a household head geographically and confirm county location; this is the closest available substitute for the missing 1790 federal census. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- Pension files at NARA (RG 15) are among the most detailed sources for Revolutionary War veterans — they often include the veteran's service narrative, family members' names and ages, and residence at application; access digitized pension files through Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- For veterans who survived the war, seek post-war bounty land warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia; these records connect veterans to their land claims in the Virginia Military District of Ohio and can confirm service. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- Virginia county boundaries shifted frequently; always confirm which county your ancestor lived in and which county held that territory at the target date, then work backward through the predecessor county's records if necessary.
- Virginia's Anglican/Episcopal vestry records served as the official civil vital record through 1784 — they are especially important for the wartime period when no civil registration existed; seek them through FamilySearch collection 1598230 and at the Library of Virginia.

Here is what the locality guide found for New Orleans in the early 1800s:

---

## New Orleans, Orleans Parish — Early 1800s: Record Survival and Substitutes

### The Disaster Context
New Orleans records were shaped by several catastrophic losses:
- **Two great fires** — 1788 and 1794 — destroyed much of the colonial city
- Repeated **yellow fever epidemics**, hurricanes, and floods also affected record-keeping institutions over the decades

Despite these losses, two major bodies of records survived and are the researcher's primary tools for this period.

---

### What Survived and Where to Find It

**1. St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers**
- Baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731** (with gaps)
- Available through FamilySearch's collection: **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"**
- These are often the only record of birth, marriage, or death for this era — vital registration did not exist in a modern sense

**2. New Orleans Notarial Archives**
- Held by the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
- Over **30 million pages from 1734** — a direct result of Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system, which required a notary for every legal transaction
- These acts record: **marriages, property sales, wills, manumissions, apprenticeships, succession proceedings** — covering people who left no vital record at all
- FamilySearch has digitized one browse-only volume covering **1803–1820** (167 images, in French and English)

---

### FamilySearch Collections to Search
- Louisiana church records
- Parish marriage records
- Probate/succession records
- A statewide death index
- New Orleans **passenger arrival lists** at NARA (for immigration)

---

### Critical Louisiana-Specific Warnings

🔑 **Louisiana uses completely different legal terminology** from every other U.S. state:
- "Probate" → **succession**
- "Guardianship" → **tutorship**
- Property transfers went through a notary, *not* a courthouse deed book

An empty search in a standard probate or deed index often means the record exists under Louisiana-specific terminology or in the **notarial archive** — not that it doesn't exist.

---

### Note on the FamilySearch Wiki
The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana (covering vital, land, church, census, probate, and New Orleans records) were unavailable during this survey. Those pages very likely exist and should be consulted by running this guide again before beginning active research.

---

### Next Steps
With this locality guide in hand, a research plan can now target:
1. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers
2. The FamilySearch Louisiana collections above
3. New Orleans passenger arrival lists (NARA)
4. The New Orleans Notarial Archives for any legal events (property, succession, manumission, etc.)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded 1718 by France; passed to Spanish control 1763; returned briefly to France before the Louisiana Purchase 1803; incorporated into the Territory of Orleans 1803–1812; became part of the State of Louisiana when Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish; Territory of Orleans (1803–1812); State of Louisiana (from 1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools for this specific city; New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. cities by mid-century with rapid growth through the 1840s–1850s driven by river commerce and immigration
- **Economy:** River trade, cotton and sugar commerce, and shipping; a dominant port at the mouth of the Mississippi
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish, African-descended (enslaved and free), Anglo-American immigrants, German and Irish immigrants (especially after 1830); a highly multilingual and multiracial population whose diversity directly shaped which languages appear in records
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (especially among Creole and French/Spanish colonial populations); Protestant denominations arrived with Anglo-American migrants after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Two devastating city fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial records; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the period (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans passed through three governing powers before American rule was established: French colonial authority (1718–1763), Spanish colonial authority (1763–1800/1803), and a brief return to French authority before the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- From 1803 to 1812 the city was the seat of the Territory of Orleans under U.S. territorial government. From 1812 onward it was part of the State of Louisiana.
- Records created before 1803 were under French or Spanish colonial authority and may be held under those predecessor jurisdictions. The same ancestor's documentary trail may cross French, Spanish, and American record-keeping systems, often in different languages and formats.
- Louisiana uses parishes (not counties) as its primary civil subdivision; Orleans Parish is the county-equivalent for record-keeping purposes.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level at which it was created is noted.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The specific Louisiana Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey (wiki-query-api outage); no registration level or year can be stated. FamilySearch collection 1543892 (Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964) indicates indexed death records begin as early as 1819, but this reflects the collection's index range, not necessarily the start of mandatory statewide registration. FamilySearch collection 1798054 (Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957) similarly shows indexed marriages from 1837. What registration level or mandate applied during the early 1800s cannot be confirmed from returned tool results.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1543892, Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892); FamilySearch collection 1798054, Louisiana Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (567,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System); FamilySearch holds indexed collections above
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many colonial-era vital records; survivorship for the earliest years of the target period is uneven
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral are the primary civil-vital substitute for the early 1800s (see Church records below); notarial acts record marriages contracted before a notary

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant; records in French and Spanish through the colonial and early American period); Protestant denominations arrived after 1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral run from 1731, though with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives (originals held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans); FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925," nearly 988,000 records (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed portions of the colonial-era sacramental registers; the surviving registers are the principal pre-civil-registration source for births, marriages, and burials
- **Language:** Records are in French and/or Spanish through the colonial and early American period; English appears increasingly after 1803

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal censuses were taken for the Louisiana territory beginning with the 1810 enumeration; Orleans Parish appears in the 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860 federal censuses
- **State/provincial census:** The specific Louisiana Census FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey; whether Louisiana conducted state enumerations in this period cannot be confirmed from returned tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) cover ancestors present before 1803 and are relevant for the earliest years of the target period
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and available at Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and also on FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses civil law (Napoleonic Code); the equivalent of probate is a "succession"; guardianship is a "tutorship"; legal incapacity proceedings are "interdictions." These are the Louisiana terms for records found elsewhere as wills, estate administrations, and guardianships (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Testate or intestate:** Whether a person left a will (testate — look for testaments within the succession file) or died without one (intestate — look for administration of succession) determines which series to search; both are part of the succession record
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984," covers the entire target period (456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (originals); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); FamilySearch collection 2078341

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot system, not the U.S. township-and-range rectangular survey; land descriptions use arpents and toises rather than acres and chains
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The specific Louisiana Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey; land grants in the colonial period were French and Spanish crown grants; U.S. federal land patents after 1803 are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Types:** Notarial acts are central to Louisiana land records — every real-property conveyance required a notarial act. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds more than 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Tax records, mortgage records, and conveyance records are also held at the parish level.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (originals; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters); FamilySearch holds one browse-only digitized volume of Notarial Acts, 1803–1820 (imageGroup 004990115, 167 images, in French and English, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Louisiana militia service; Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Louisiana militia records; War of 1812 records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA; https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), No. 2 (1823), and No. 3 (1854) are the primary Catholic above-ground burial sites in New Orleans; Protestant and other cemeteries also existed in the period
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed memorials for New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers; some may be held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active newspapers throughout the period (including the Louisiana Gazette from ca. 1804); papers published legal notices, succession announcements, ship arrivals, and vital notices
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; the Historic New Orleans Collection and Tulane University also hold newspaper holdings
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate/succession notices, and published ship-arrival passenger lists (naming immigrants)

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was itself a major port of entry — one of the busiest U.S. ports of entry by the 1830s–1850s; immigrants arrived from France, Germany, Ireland, and elsewhere
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (manifests); naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record — Orleans Parish courts and U.S. District Court for Louisiana); declarations of intention
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists; FamilySearch and Ancestry.com also hold indexed passenger list collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and poll tax records were maintained at the parish level
- **Date range:** Spanish colonial tax lists (padrones) exist for the period before 1803; American-era tax records begin with territorial administration (1803+)
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and confirm residence and property holdings

### Other record types
- **Notarial records (central to Louisiana research):** Every legal transaction — contracts, sales, partnerships, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons, apprenticeships, and marriage contracts — required a notarial act in Louisiana. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the largest surviving body. FamilySearch's one digitized volume (imageGroup 004990115, 1803–1820) must be browsed image-by-image; it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. The researcher must read French and/or English to use it.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records 1718–1925 (1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records 1756–1984 (2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 (1543892); Notarial Acts browse-only volume (imageGroup 004990115, 1803–1820) | Church sacramentals; successions/probate; death index; notarial acts 1803–1820 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census (1810–1860); passenger arrival lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records | War of 1812; Louisiana militia records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records | Cemetery memorials and burial information for New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Vital notices, legal notices, succession announcements in New Orleans papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; naturalization records; federal records | Port-of-New-Orleans arrivals; U.S. federal land patents | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for the Orleans/Louisiana area and time period (Notarial Acts 1803–1820, imageGroup 004990115, 167 images, browse-only). This was the complete result set returned. Additional digitized material at the state level may not have surfaced in this city-level query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (originals) | In-person; some microfilm copies |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records; successions; tax records; militia records | In-person; online request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; other Catholic parish registers | In-person; contact archives |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Maps, manuscripts, newspapers, photographs | In-person research center |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) records; court minutes; naturalizations | In-person |

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded 1718 by France; passed to Spanish control 1763; returned briefly to France before the Louisiana Purchase 1803; incorporated into the Territory of Orleans 1803–1812; became part of the State of Louisiana when Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish; Territory of Orleans (1803–1812); State of Louisiana (from 1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools for this specific city; New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. cities by mid-century with rapid growth through the 1840s–1850s driven by river commerce and immigration
- **Economy:** River trade, cotton and sugar commerce, and shipping; a dominant port at the mouth of the Mississippi
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish, African-descended (enslaved and free), Anglo-American immigrants, German and Irish immigrants (especially after 1830); a highly multilingual and multiracial population whose diversity directly shaped which languages appear in records
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (especially among Creole and French/Spanish colonial populations); Protestant denominations arrived with Anglo-American migrants after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Two devastating city fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial records; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the period (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans passed through three governing powers before American rule was established: French colonial authority (1718–1763), Spanish colonial authority (1763–1800/1803), and a brief return to French authority before the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- From 1803 to 1812 the city was the seat of the Territory of Orleans under U.S. territorial government. From 1812 onward it was part of the State of Louisiana.
- Records created before 1803 were under French or Spanish colonial authority and may be held under those predecessor jurisdictions. The same ancestor's documentary trail may cross French, Spanish, and American record-keeping systems, often in different languages and formats.
- Louisiana uses parishes (not counties) as its primary civil subdivision; Orleans Parish is the county-equivalent for record-keeping purposes.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level at which it was created is noted.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The specific Louisiana Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey (wiki-query-api outage); no registration level or year can be stated. FamilySearch collection 1543892 (Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964) indicates indexed death records begin as early as 1819, but this reflects the collection's index range, not necessarily the start of mandatory statewide registration. FamilySearch collection 1798054 (Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957) similarly shows indexed marriages from 1837. What registration level or mandate applied during the early 1800s cannot be confirmed from returned tool results.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1543892, Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892); FamilySearch collection 1798054, Louisiana Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (567,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System); FamilySearch holds indexed collections above
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many colonial-era vital records; survivorship for the earliest years of the target period is uneven
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral are the primary civil-vital substitute for the early 1800s (see Church records below); notarial acts record marriages contracted before a notary

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant; records in French and Spanish through the colonial and early American period); Protestant denominations arrived after 1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral run from 1731, though with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives (originals held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans); FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925," nearly 988,000 records (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed portions of the colonial-era sacramental registers; the surviving registers are the principal pre-civil-registration source for births, marriages, and burials
- **Language:** Records are in French and/or Spanish through the colonial and early American period; English appears increasingly after 1803

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal censuses were taken for the Louisiana territory beginning with the 1810 enumeration; Orleans Parish appears in the 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860 federal censuses
- **State/provincial census:** The specific Louisiana Census FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey; whether Louisiana conducted state enumerations in this period cannot be confirmed from returned tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) cover ancestors present before 1803 and are relevant for the earliest years of the target period
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and available at Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and also on FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses civil law (Napoleonic Code); the equivalent of probate is a "succession"; guardianship is a "tutorship"; legal incapacity proceedings are "interdictions." These are the Louisiana terms for records found elsewhere as wills, estate administrations, and guardianships (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Testate or intestate:** Whether a person left a will (testate — look for testaments within the succession file) or died without one (intestate — look for administration of succession) determines which series to search; both are part of the succession record
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341, "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984," covers the entire target period (456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (originals); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); FamilySearch collection 2078341

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot system, not the U.S. township-and-range rectangular survey; land descriptions use arpents and toises rather than acres and chains
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The specific Louisiana Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey; land grants in the colonial period were French and Spanish crown grants; U.S. federal land patents after 1803 are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (https://www.glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Types:** Notarial acts are central to Louisiana land records — every real-property conveyance required a notarial act. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds more than 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Tax records, mortgage records, and conveyance records are also held at the parish level.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (originals; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters); FamilySearch holds one browse-only digitized volume of Notarial Acts, 1803–1820 (imageGroup 004990115, 167 images, in French and English, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Louisiana militia service; Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Louisiana militia records; War of 1812 records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA; https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), No. 2 (1823), and No. 3 (1854) are the primary Catholic above-ground burial sites in New Orleans; Protestant and other cemeteries also existed in the period
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed memorials for New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers; some may be held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active newspapers throughout the period (including the Louisiana Gazette from ca. 1804); papers published legal notices, succession announcements, ship arrivals, and vital notices
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; the Historic New Orleans Collection and Tulane University also hold newspaper holdings
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate/succession notices, and published ship-arrival passenger lists (naming immigrants)

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was itself a major port of entry — one of the busiest U.S. ports of entry by the 1830s–1850s; immigrants arrived from France, Germany, Ireland, and elsewhere
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (manifests); naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record — Orleans Parish courts and U.S. District Court for Louisiana); declarations of intention
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists; FamilySearch and Ancestry.com also hold indexed passenger list collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and poll tax records were maintained at the parish level
- **Date range:** Spanish colonial tax lists (padrones) exist for the period before 1803; American-era tax records begin with territorial administration (1803+)
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and confirm residence and property holdings

### Other record types
- **Notarial records (central to Louisiana research):** Every legal transaction — contracts, sales, partnerships, wills, manumissions of enslaved persons, apprenticeships, and marriage contracts — required a notarial act in Louisiana. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the largest surviving body. FamilySearch's one digitized volume (imageGroup 004990115, 1803–1820) must be browsed image-by-image; it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. The researcher must read French and/or English to use it.

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston, Massachusetts (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts; settled 1630
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (county seat of Suffolk County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Massachusetts; federal customs authority governed the port
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by the tool for this period
- **Economy:** Major seaport; shipbuilding, commerce, textile trade
- **Ethnic composition:** By 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852); earlier Irish arrivals and smaller German, British, and Canadian communities also present (Wikipedia)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish immigrants); Protestant denominations including Congregational, Episcopalian, Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove mass Irish migration; tens of thousands arrived through Boston in the 1840s

## Boundary changes
- Suffolk County was established in 1643 as one of Massachusetts' original counties; Boston's boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s
- No jurisdictional boundary changes directly affect records in the target period

## Available record types

### Immigration and emigration records (primary record class for this research question)
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston (primary); some immigrants arrived via Canadian ports (Halifax, Quebec) and continued overland or by coasting vessel
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (1820–1891) in NARA Record Group 36; FamilySearch collection 1784312 "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (1,234,567 records) indexes them: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312
- **1840s list contents:** 1840s customs passenger lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not hometown or relatives' names (FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Immigration," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Digitized volume:** 1 volume confirmed for 1840–1850 (image group 003345210, 389 images) — full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed; use full-text search, not a name index
- **Originals held at:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), which holds NARA Record Group 36 for the Port of Boston
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents; examine the full manifest for all family members

### Naturalization records
- **Types:** Declarations of intention (first papers), petitions for naturalization; pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize
- **FamilySearch collection:** 1459213 "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (345,678 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Where held:** National Archives at Boston and Massachusetts State Archives hold court naturalization series; also county and local courts

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level and start date:** The Massachusetts Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content during this survey; this guide cannot state when civil registration began or at what level from tool results
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550 "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (3,456,789 records) covers the period; records were kept at the **town** level — search Boston as a town: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers; The Pilot newspaper notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Congregational, Episcopalian, Methodist, and Baptist for earlier Yankee populations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** Catholic parish registers — including those of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's — are held at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Church Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston); FamilySearch collection 1921657 "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (987,654 records) is indexed with images: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Language:** English; some Catholic sacramental registers in Latin

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 and 1850 censuses cover Boston; the 1840 census lists only heads of household by age bracket, the 1850 census names every household member
- **State census:** This survey did not confirm a Massachusetts state census for the 1840s from tool results
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (567,890 records) covers the period: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court in Boston; FamilySearch for digitized records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town and county level; the Massachusetts Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page was not fetched during this survey — this guide cannot state which office holds grants/patents from tool results
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; Massachusetts State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) for immigrants who settled and later served
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files at NARA; state adjutant general records at Massachusetts State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Old Granary Burying Ground, Copp's Hill Burying Ground, Forest Hills Cemetery, Holy Cross Cemetery
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers — specific availability not confirmed by this survey's tool results

### Newspaper records
- **Key paper:** The Pilot (Boston Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements; a primary resource for Irish Famine immigrants (Wikipedia)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Boston Public Library historical collection; Boston College Burns Library holds a digitized edition
- **Content value:** Missing-persons notices sometimes name the Irish parish of origin — search before concluding a passenger list entry cannot be further identified

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, poll tax at town and county level
- **Where held:** Massachusetts State Archives; city/town level
- **Substitute value:** Can help locate immigrants between census years

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (collection 1784312); Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (2061550); Church Records, 1630–1920 (1921657); Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (1459213); Probate Records, 1635–1991 (1678901) | Core immigration, vital, church, and naturalization records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records; Boston passenger list indexes | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Record Group 36 — Port of Boston customs passenger lists (originals and digital finding aids) | Original arrival manifests; pre-1906 naturalizations | Free / in-person |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records not fully indexed elsewhere | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | The Pilot missing-persons notices; obituaries | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service records, pension files | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the Port of Boston passenger list series for 1840–1850 (image group 003345210, 389 images); this was the complete result returned by the volume search. The broader Massachusetts Passenger Lists collection (1784312) covers 1820–1891 but its internal volume breakdown was not examined in full.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists (RG 36); pre-1906 naturalization records | In-person / NARA research services |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers from the 1840s onward, including Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's | Contact the archives directly |
| Massachusetts State Archives | Court records, probate, state vital records | In-person / mail request |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds | Deed books, mortgages | In-person / county website |
| Boston Public Library | Local newspapers, city directories, local history | In-person / some digitized |
| Boston College Burns Library | Digitized edition of The Pilot newspaper | Online / in-person |

## Records NOT online
- Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists at National Archives at Boston (Waltham) — the FamilySearch digitized volume (image group 003345210) is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed; a name search requires the full-text interface
- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or digitized — physical access to the archives is required
- Port quarantine and health inspection records — repositories not confirmed by this survey's tool results
- FamilySearch Catalog search was not available during this survey; additional microfilm holdings may exist and are not reflected here

## Known record losses
- No specific record losses for Port of Boston 1840s immigration records were reported in this survey's tool results

## Research tips
- Begin with the FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312); the 1840–1850 digitized volume (image group 003345210) is full-text searchable. Use the ship name and arrival date to locate the full manifest and identify other family members who traveled together. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- Catholic parish records are essential when passenger lists give only "Ireland" as country of origin. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds registers for the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and other early parishes; FamilySearch collection 1921657 also indexes Massachusetts church records. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- Search The Pilot newspaper's missing-persons column before concluding a passenger list entry cannot be further identified — notices sometimes name the Irish county or parish of origin.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations occurred in any court of record. Search FamilySearch collection 1459213 and also the court minute books at the National Archives at Boston and Massachusetts State Archives.
- Massachusetts vital records in this period were kept at the town level — search Boston as a town in collection 2061550, not at the Suffolk County level.
- The 1850 federal census is the first to name every household member; for immigrants who arrived mid-to-late 1840s, it may capture the family's composition shortly after arrival — cross-reference with the passenger list.

## Oklahoma / Indian Territory — Tribal Records Locality Guide (Mid-1800s)

### Jurisdiction and Historical Context

The area was called **Indian Territory** during the mid-1800s — Oklahoma as a state didn't exist until 1907. It was home to the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole), who were forcibly relocated there under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Because no county government or civil vital registration existed during this period, you must look to substitute record types.

---

### Key Record Types

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Tribal enrollment rolls** | 1851 onward | The primary substitute for vital records |
| **BIA annuity payment lists** | Ongoing from removal era | Lists heads of household by tribe |
| **Missionary church registers** | 1820 onward | Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missions |
| **Tribal censuses** | 1851 onward | Name-indexed on FamilySearch |
| **Early land records** | 1834 onward | Available on FamilySearch |

---

### FamilySearch Collections (Confirmed)

Three collections cover the target period and are name-indexed and free on FamilySearch:
- **Tribal censuses and rolls** (1851 onward) — 567,890 persons
- **Early land records** (1834 onward) — 234,567 persons
- **Mission and church records** (1820 onward) — 123,456 persons

For mid-century research, start with the **Old Settler Cherokee Roll of 1851** or the **Drennen Roll of 1852**, found in FamilySearch collection **1987432**.

---

### Physical Repositories

- **National Archives — Fort Worth, Texas**: Holds original BIA agency records, the Dawes Rolls, and tribal court records
- **Ancestry / Fold3**: Some of the same material is indexed on these platforms

---

### Two Critical Cautions

1. **Follow the removal trail backward**: Every research path in Indian Territory must also run into the southeastern state the family was removed from — **Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, or Florida** — because that is where earlier records are held.

2. **Identify the tribe first**: The record sets are tribe-specific. Determine which tribal nation the ancestor belonged to before searching, since rolls and agencies were organized by tribe.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Identify the specific tribal nation(s) connected to your ancestor.
2. Search the tribe-specific enrollment rolls on FamilySearch, beginning with the mid-1800s rolls noted above.
3. Simultaneously locate the family's **pre-removal records** in the appropriate southeastern state.
4. Check the **FamilySearch Research Wiki** directly at familysearch.org/wiki for tribe-specific guidance pages, as they may hold additional detail.
