entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s, approximately 1830–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory established under the Indian Removal Act of 1830; Oklahoma achieved statehood in 1907 — the entire mid-1800s target period falls under federal and tribal authority, not state or county government
- **Administrative center:** No county-seat structure; tribal nations (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) maintained their own governments; the Bureau of Indian Affairs administered agency offices
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States federal government
- **Population during period:** Population data were not returned for Indian Territory from the available tools for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, herding, and trade among relocated tribal nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) were the principal groups after removal; African-descended enslaved persons and freedmen also present; white missionaries and traders in limited numbers
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionary churches established from the 1820s onward (confirmed: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removals under Indian Removal Act of 1830 (tribal removals occurred through the 1830s–1840s); Civil War (1861–1865) disrupted records and divided tribal loyalties

## Boundary changes
- Before 1830: unorganized federal land west of Arkansas and Missouri
- 1830 onward: designated Indian Territory for tribal relocation; not an organized U.S. territory in the standard sense — tribal nations held governing authority over their own districts
- 1907: Oklahoma statehood; county government and state registration systems began at that point
- Records from the mid-1800s fall under tribal and federal, not state or county, jurisdiction — the standard county-based research approach does not apply
- Pre-removal records for the Five Civilized Tribes are held in the southeastern states of origin: Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Florida

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the mid-1800s; Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return specific vital registration dates for Oklahoma during this survey (the wiki pages returned only generic content)
- **What exists:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths for the mid-1800s target period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls, BIA agency annuity records, and missionary church registers are the functional equivalents for vital events

### Tribal enrollment records (primary source for this period)
- **What exists:** Tribal enrollment cards and census rolls. FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432) covers 567,890 persons and is available online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432. Volume search confirmed 1 digitized volume (image group 002298871, 940 images) of tribal enrollment cards for Indian Territory 1840–1870; this volume is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.
- **Earlier rolls within the target period:** The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) are among the mid-century rolls (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Postdate the target period but are retrospective and name family members; indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; originals at NARA Fort Worth (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward; kept registers of converts, students, and community members (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; original registers at denominational archives
- **Gaps:** Not all missionary registers are confirmed as covered by this collection; undigitized registers remain at denominational archives
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records
- **What exists:** Annuity payment rolls, agency correspondence, school records, and census enumerations maintained by BIA agents for each tribal nation
- **Where held:** National Archives — Fort Worth, TX (NARA), per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records; some records accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and FamilySearch
- **Digitization level:** Partial — some records online; physical access at NARA Fort Worth for undigitized material

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Tribal common lands, not General Land Office rectangular survey, during the mid-1800s target period; allotment under the Dawes Act did not begin until 1887
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Tribal governments held authority over land assignments within each nation's boundaries during this period. The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records) is available at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1541872 (online); originals at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Indian Territory was not enumerated in standard federal censuses for 1840 or 1850 as a state or organized territory. Special Indian censuses were taken by the BIA and are included in FamilySearch collection 1987432
- **Other enumerations:** Annuity payment rolls and tribal census lists functioned as de facto enumerations; part of BIA agency records at NARA Fort Worth
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1987432)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal nations maintained their own courts with jurisdiction over wills, estates, and civil disputes; these records are separate from U.S. court probate records
- **Where held:** Tribal court records at NARA Fort Worth and at individual tribal archives; not confirmed as a standalone digitized collection by this survey
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical only or microfilm at NARA

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Cherokee, Creek, and other tribes supplied soldiers to both Union and Confederate sides; records for tribal military service are at NARA
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records including some tribal service documentation
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 online

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) includes Indian Territory/Oklahoma cemeteries; mid-1800s coverage is sparse
- **Physical records:** Tribal burial grounds and mission cemetery registers; no specific digitized burial register collection for mid-1800s Indian Territory was confirmed by this survey

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Tribal newspapers such as the Cherokee Phoenix and its successors published notices and legal proceedings; this survey did not return specific newspaper holdings for Indian Territory from tool results
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society and University of Oklahoma hold some tribal newspaper archives; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) covers some period titles

### Immigration and removal records
- **Relevant movements:** The forced removals of the 1830s–1840s from southeastern states are documented in treaty records, removal rolls, and emigration lists at NARA; these are critically important — the family's pre-Oklahoma trail begins in the state of origin
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); some removal records are indexed in FamilySearch's tribal rolls collection
- **Content note:** Removal rolls name every person — including infants and young children — who made the journey. Examine the full roll for all family members, not just the head of household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tribal nations levied their own taxes and assessments; part of tribal government records at NARA Fort Worth and tribal archives
- **Date range:** Varies by nation; not confirmed as a standalone digitized collection by this survey

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (1987432); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (1654321) | Tribal enrollment, land, and church records | Free |
| NARA | BIA agency records, Dawes Rolls, removal records, tribal court records | Unindexed BIA correspondence, full allotment files, records not in FamilySearch | In-person and online request (https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Ancestry | Tribal rolls and Dawes Rolls index (noted in FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls) | Supplemental tribal roll index | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military records including some tribal Civil War service | Civil War tribal service records not online elsewhere | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Oklahoma/Indian Territory | Burial information | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matched the Indian Territory query for 1840–1870 (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% indexed). The collections search returned 3 collections overlapping the target period. These are the complete results returned — no additional pages were withheld.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives — Fort Worth, TX | Dawes Rolls, BIA agency records, tribal court records, removal records | In-person or NARA online request (archives.gov) |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS) | Oklahoma and Indian Territory records, tribal records, newspapers | In-person; some holdings online |
| Tribal archives (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole nations) | Tribal government records, genealogical services | Contact each nation directly |
| State archives in GA, AL, MS, TN, FL | Pre-removal records for tribal members before the 1830s removals | In-person or state archives request |

## Records NOT online
- Tribal court probate and civil records — physical at NARA Fort Worth and tribal archives
- Full BIA agency correspondence files — at NARA, not fully digitized
- Pre-removal records from southeastern origin states — at those states' archives
- Tribal nation tax and assessment records
- Missionary church registers not covered by FamilySearch collection 1654321

## Known record losses
- The Civil War (1861–1865) disrupted records across Indian Territory; some tribal government records were damaged or lost. This survey did not locate a specific tool result confirming the precise extent of losses — contact NARA Fort Worth and individual tribal archives for confirmation.
- The FamilySearch Wiki specific Oklahoma pages returned only generic content during this survey; confirmed record-loss information from those pages is not available from this run.

## Research tips
- Begin with the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), the most widely used enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes, indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; use them to identify ancestors and work backward to mid-century family members (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- For the mid-1800s target period specifically, check the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) as primary enrollment sources (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- Pre-removal records are equally important: the family's trail leads back to the southeastern state of origin — search Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, or Florida records depending on the tribe
- BIA agency records (annuity payment rolls, school records, census lists) at NARA Fort Worth name individuals who may not appear on formal enrollment rolls; treat them as a supplement, not a substitute (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- Missionary records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) name converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward; check FamilySearch collection 1654321 and also contact denominational archives for registers not yet digitized (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- Indian Territory bordered Arkansas to the east and Kansas to the north; families near those borders generated records on both sides — Arkansas court and land records processed many removal-era documents
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Oklahoma (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey; check those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki before concluding they have no Oklahoma-specific guidance

The original BIA agency records, the Dawes Rolls, and tribal court records are held physically at the National Archives in Fort Worth, Texas, with some material also indexed on Ancestry and Fold3. The two most important cautions are: first, every research trail in Indian Territory must also run backward into the southeastern state the family was removed from — Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, or Florida — because that is where the earlier records are; and second, the FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Oklahoma all returned only generic content during this survey, so check them directly at familysearch.org/wiki before concluding they offer nothing further.

The next step is to identify which tribal nation or nations the ancestor belonged to, then search the tribe-specific enrollment rolls (starting with the Old Settler Cherokee Roll of 1851 or the Drennen Roll of 1852 for mid-century research) in FamilySearch collection 1987432, and simultaneously locate the family's pre-removal records in the appropriate southeastern state.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s, approximately 1830–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory established under the Indian Removal Act of 1830; Oklahoma achieved statehood in 1907 — the entire mid-1800s target period falls under federal and tribal authority, not state or county government
- **Administrative center:** No county-seat structure; tribal nations (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) maintained their own governments; the Bureau of Indian Affairs administered agency offices
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States federal government
- **Population during period:** Population data were not returned for Indian Territory from the available tools for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, herding, and trade among relocated tribal nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) were the principal groups after removal; African-descended enslaved persons and freedmen also present; white missionaries and traders in limited numbers
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionary churches established from the 1820s onward (confirmed: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removals under Indian Removal Act of 1830 (tribal removals occurred through the 1830s–1840s); Civil War (1861–1865) disrupted records and divided tribal loyalties

## Boundary changes
- Before 1830: unorganized federal land west of Arkansas and Missouri
- 1830 onward: designated Indian Territory for tribal relocation; not an organized U.S. territory in the standard sense — tribal nations held governing authority over their own districts
- 1907: Oklahoma statehood; county government and state registration systems began at that point
- Records from the mid-1800s fall under tribal and federal, not state or county, jurisdiction — the standard county-based research approach does not apply
- Pre-removal records for the Five Civilized Tribes are held in the southeastern states of origin: Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Florida

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the mid-1800s; Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return specific vital registration dates for Oklahoma during this survey (the wiki pages returned only generic content)
- **What exists:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths for the mid-1800s target period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls, BIA agency annuity records, and missionary church registers are the functional equivalents for vital events

### Tribal enrollment records (primary source for this period)
- **What exists:** Tribal enrollment cards and census rolls. FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432) covers 567,890 persons and is available online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432. Volume search confirmed 1 digitized volume (image group 002298871, 940 images) of tribal enrollment cards for Indian Territory 1840–1870; this volume is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.
- **Earlier rolls within the target period:** The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) are among the mid-century rolls (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Postdate the target period but are retrospective and name family members; indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; originals at NARA Fort Worth (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward; kept registers of converts, students, and community members (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; original registers at denominational archives
- **Gaps:** Not all missionary registers are confirmed as covered by this collection; undigitized registers remain at denominational archives
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records
- **What exists:** Annuity payment rolls, agency correspondence, school records, and census enumerations maintained by BIA agents for each tribal nation
- **Where held:** National Archives — Fort Worth, TX (NARA), per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records; some records accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and FamilySearch
- **Digitization level:** Partial — some records online; physical access at NARA Fort Worth for undigitized material

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Tribal common lands, not General Land Office rectangular survey, during the mid-1800s target period; allotment under the Dawes Act did not begin until 1887
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Tribal governments held authority over land assignments within each nation's boundaries during this period. The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records) is available at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1541872 (online); originals at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Indian Territory was not enumerated in standard federal censuses for 1840 or 1850 as a state or organized territory. Special Indian censuses were taken by the BIA and are included in FamilySearch collection 1987432
- **Other enumerations:** Annuity payment rolls and tribal census lists functioned as de facto enumerations; part of BIA agency records at NARA Fort Worth
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1987432)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal nations maintained their own courts with jurisdiction over wills, estates, and civil disputes; these records are separate from U.S. court probate records
- **Where held:** Tribal court records at NARA Fort Worth and at individual tribal archives; not confirmed as a standalone digitized collection by this survey
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical only or microfilm at NARA

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Cherokee, Creek, and other tribes supplied soldiers to both Union and Confederate sides; records for tribal military service are at NARA
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records including some tribal service documentation
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 online

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) includes Indian Territory/Oklahoma cemeteries; mid-1800s coverage is sparse
- **Physical records:** Tribal burial grounds and mission cemetery registers; no specific digitized burial register collection for mid-1800s Indian Territory was confirmed by this survey

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Tribal newspapers such as the Cherokee Phoenix and its successors published notices and legal proceedings; this survey did not return specific newspaper holdings for Indian Territory from tool results
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society and University of Oklahoma hold some tribal newspaper archives; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) covers some period titles

### Immigration and removal records
- **Relevant movements:** The forced removals of the 1830s–1840s from southeastern states are documented in treaty records, removal rolls, and emigration lists at NARA; these are critically important — the family's pre-Oklahoma trail begins in the state of origin
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); some removal records are indexed in FamilySearch's tribal rolls collection
- **Content note:** Removal rolls name every person — including infants and young children — who made the journey. Examine the full roll for all family members, not just the head of household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tribal nations levied their own taxes and assessments; part of tribal government records at NARA Fort Worth and tribal archives
- **Date range:** Varies by nation; not confirmed as a standalone digitized collection by this survey

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (1987432); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (1654321) | Tribal enrollment, land, and church records | Free |
| NARA | BIA agency records, Dawes Rolls, removal records, tribal court records | Unindexed BIA correspondence, full allotment files, records not in FamilySearch | In-person and online request (https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Ancestry | Tribal rolls and Dawes Rolls index (noted in FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls) | Supplemental tribal roll index | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military records including some tribal Civil War service | Civil War tribal service records not online elsewhere | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Oklahoma/Indian Territory | Burial information | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matched the Indian Territory query for 1840–1870 (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% indexed). The collections search returned 3 collections overlapping the target period. These are the complete results returned — no additional pages were withheld.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives — Fort Worth, TX | Dawes Rolls, BIA agency records, tribal court records, removal records | In-person or NARA online request (archives.gov) |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS) | Oklahoma and Indian Territory records, tribal records, newspapers | In-person; some holdings online |
| Tribal archives (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole nations) | Tribal government records, genealogical services | Contact each nation directly |
| State archives in GA, AL, MS, TN, FL | Pre-removal records for tribal members before the 1830s removals | In-person or state archives request |

## Records NOT online
- Tribal court probate and civil records — physical at NARA Fort Worth and tribal archives
- Full BIA agency correspondence files — at NARA, not fully digitized
- Pre-removal records from southeastern origin states — at those states' archives
- Tribal nation tax and assessment records
- Missionary church registers not covered by FamilySearch collection 1654321

## Known record losses
- The Civil War (1861–1865) disrupted records across Indian Territory; some tribal government records were damaged or lost. This survey did not locate a specific tool result confirming the precise extent of losses — contact NARA Fort Worth and individual tribal archives for confirmation.
- The FamilySearch Wiki specific Oklahoma pages returned only generic content during this survey; confirmed record-loss information from those pages is not available from this run.

## Research tips
- Begin with the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), the most widely used enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes, indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; use them to identify ancestors and work backward to mid-century family members (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- For the mid-1800s target period specifically, check the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) as primary enrollment sources (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- Pre-removal records are equally important: the family's trail leads back to the southeastern state of origin — search Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, or Florida records depending on the tribe
- BIA agency records (annuity payment rolls, school records, census lists) at NARA Fort Worth name individuals who may not appear on formal enrollment rolls; treat them as a supplement, not a substitute (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- Missionary records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) name converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward; check FamilySearch collection 1654321 and also contact denominational archives for registers not yet digitized (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- Indian Territory bordered Arkansas to the east and Kansas to the north; families near those borders generated records on both sides — Arkansas court and land records processed many removal-era documents
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Oklahoma (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey; check those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki before concluding they have no Oklahoma-specific guidance

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had no statewide civil registration for births or deaths — that did not come until 1906 — so **Quaker monthly meeting records are, in practical terms, the vital records** for that era and community. Those records (births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal when a family moved to another meeting, and disownment proceedings) are held primarily at:

- **Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College** — the largest U.S. collection of Quaker records, with FamilySearch microfilm covering many individual meetings.
- **FamilySearch** holds one digitized volume: *Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800* (145 browse-only images, no name index).
- **County marriage licenses** (colonial period) are searchable in FamilySearch collections 1571957 and 1502909.
- **Probate records from 1683 onward** are in FamilySearch collection 1999196 (3.2 million browse-only images).

**Key census substitute:** Because there is no Pennsylvania census before 1790, county tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward are the primary census substitute.

**Important caveat:** Quaker records follow the **monthly meeting's jurisdiction, not county lines**, so you must identify the specific meeting before searching. **William Wade Hinshaw's six-volume *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** is the indexed starting point for that before going to the originals at Swarthmore or on microfilm.

**Next step:** Identify which Quaker monthly meeting served the specific Pennsylvania community where your ancestors lived, then locate that meeting's registers on FamilySearch microfilm or at the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States (1750–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1681 as a proprietary colony under William Penn; became a state in 1787
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial era); Harrisburg (capital from 1799)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial period); United States (post-1776)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned for this period by the survey tools
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron manufacturing, trade, timber; Philadelphia was the dominant commercial center of colonial North America
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (founding population), German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite, Amish), Scots-Irish (Presbyterian), Welsh, Dutch, Swedish, and Irish communities
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Amish, Catholic, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) disrupted record-keeping in some areas; the Wyoming Valley was in dispute with Connecticut until the Trenton Decree (1782)

## Boundary changes
- County formation was rapid throughout the late 1700s; new counties were carved from older ones, and records before a county's formation date must be sought in the predecessor county
- When a county was newly formed, the Register of Wills, Recorder of Deeds, and other county officers began their own series from that date; earlier records for the same territory remain in the parent county
- Pennsylvania's outer boundaries were largely fixed by the late 1700s; the Wyoming Valley dispute with Connecticut was resolved in Pennsylvania's favor by 1782

Here is the locality guide produced for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (c. 1860–1910):

---

## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Era Locality Guide

### Key Context

- **Vital registration gaps:** Civil birth and death registration in Allegheny County did not begin until 1870, and statewide registration only started in 1906. For most of the steel boom era, **church baptism and burial registers are the primary source of vital events**, not government certificates.
- **Allegheny City:** Anyone living on what is now Pittsburgh's North Side before 1907 would appear in records under **"Allegheny city"** — a separate municipality until it was annexed by Pittsburgh that year.

---

### Occupational & Industrial Sources

| Source | Held at / Access |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Pittsburgh city directories** (listing occupation and address, 1813 onward, issued annually) | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |
| **Company employment records** (fragmentary) | Senator John Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives |
| **Federal census occupation columns** (1870, 1880, 1900, 1910) | FamilySearch, Ancestry |

City directories are the highest-yield first step — they anchor a subject year-by-year with occupation and address before census years.

---

### Vital & Church Records

- **Ethnic Catholic parishes** are critical for immigrant steelworkers. Each nationality (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) maintained **separate registers**. Originals are mostly held physically at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**.
- Protestant and other denominational records vary widely by congregation.

---

### Naturalization Records

- **Allegheny County naturalizations (1798–1930)** are at the **National Archives, Philadelphia region**.
- These often name the immigrant's **specific place of origin** — the key to opening research in the home country.

---

### Census Records

- The **1880 census** is the most complete for the core steel era and includes birthplace of parents.
- The **1900 census** adds immigration year and years in the United States.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **City directories** (Carnegie Library) — anchor the subject by year, confirm occupation and address
2. **1880 and 1900 federal censuses** — family data, immigration year, parents' birthplaces
3. **Naturalization records** (NARA Philadelphia) — country and region of origin
4. **Ethnic parish registers** (Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives) — baptism, marriage, burial
5. **Company/employment records** (Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel) — industrial corroboration

---

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Allegheny County at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) is worth consulting directly for additional collection listings. This guide was saved as **loc_001** in your project.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No indexed population data was returned by tools; Pittsburgh was among the largest U.S. cities by 1900, with Allegheny County's population driven by the steel boom
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated from the 1870s onward; Carnegie Steel and related firms made Pittsburgh the center of American steel production, attracting massive immigrant labor flows (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants poured into the city and surrounding mill towns during the late 1800s
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (with numerous ethnic parishes organized by nationality), mainline Protestant; ethnic Catholic parishes were the primary record-keeping institutions for many immigrant families
- **Key historical events:** Steel industry boom of the 1870s–1900s drove massive immigration; the Homestead Strike (1892) is a notable event affecting labor records

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since its formation in 1788.
- The city of Allegheny (across the Ohio and Allegheny rivers from Pittsburgh) was a separate municipality until annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Records for residents of what is now Pittsburgh's North Side were created under "Allegheny city" jurisdictional headings before 1907 — a critical distinction when searching vital, court, and directory records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates:** Allegheny County recorded births and deaths at the **county level from 1870** — earlier than Pennsylvania's statewide mandate. Statewide civil registration began in **1906** for births and deaths. Marriage licenses at the county courthouse from **1885**. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records); [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **What exists:** County-level birth and death records 1870–1905 (at the Allegheny County courthouse); statewide death certificates 1906–1968 on FamilySearch (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed with images); county marriage licenses from 1885 (coll. 1921317, 524,189 records)
- **Where held:** County records at the Allegheny County courthouse; statewide death certificates at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration exists before 1870 at any level for Allegheny County; the statewide series begins only in 1906.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary source before 1870 and for many families between 1870 and 1906.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes: Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish, with registers from the 1840s onward); mainline Protestant. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Originals for many Catholic parishes are at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**; FamilySearch has microfilmed some registers. Identify the specific ethnic parish before searching.
- **Gaps:** Protestant parish coverage varies by congregation; surviving registers must be identified parish by parish. No comprehensive online index exists for Allegheny County parish registers.
- **Language:** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and German parishes often kept registers in their national language — these records require reading the original.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Records for Allegheny County survive from 1800. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are most valuable for steel-era workers: both record occupation and birthplace of parents; 1900 also records immigration year. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no regular state census during this period; tax assessment lists serve as intercensal substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census — the 1870 and 1880 rounds cover the early steel era.
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, letters of administration
- **Date range:** From colonial period; Allegheny County from 1788
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (courthouse); FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3,200,560 images but is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Search wills first; if none, look for administration records for the same estate.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's grants in 1681 onward. County deeds begin at Allegheny County's formation in 1788. ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax assessment lists
- **Date range:** County deeds from 1788; state land office records from 1681
- **Where held:** Deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds; state patents at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865), Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era), draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds service and pension records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has many indexed military records online; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive coverage of Pittsburgh-area cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries and church burial grounds; ethnic Catholic cemeteries often have burial registers at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily papers in the late 1800s. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pittsburgh newspapers; the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh also holds local papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news (especially Homestead Strike coverage), legal notices, naturalization announcements

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived via East Coast ports (New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore); passenger lists are at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; naturalization petitions (pre-1906 at any court of record); Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia; FamilySearch has Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (1790–1915), 15% indexed, 351 images browsable.
- **Immigration to Pittsburgh's mills:** Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia document the massive immigration to the steel mills. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. The 1880 and 1900 censuses record immigration year, providing a cross-reference for family arrival windows.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property assessment lists, personal property lists
- **Date range:** County tax lists from 1788; Pennsylvania tax lists survive from the 1690s in some counties ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists serve as census substitutes between federal enumerations and document property ownership

### Other record types — industrial and occupational sources

This is the most distinctive record category for Pittsburgh in this period and deserves priority attention:

- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary records from Carnegie Steel and related firms survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel** archives. These are not comprehensively indexed — contact both repositories directly. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **Union membership lists:** Steelworkers' union records may survive at the United Steelworkers archives or the Heinz History Center; availability is fragmentary.
- **City directories:** Pittsburgh city directories begin in 1813 and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; directories from the 1870s–1900s list occupations and home addresses, making them an indispensable year-by-year tracking tool for steel-era workers. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published reports in the late 1800s that may name specific workers or list workforce demographics; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Federal census occupation columns:** Every federal census from 1870 to 1900 records occupation; "iron puddler," "steel roller," and similar entries identify steel-era workers specifically.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (coll. 2255317) — 4.2M records | Deaths from 1906 onward | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (coll. 1921317) — 524K records | Marriages from 1885 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957) — 312K records | Earlier marriage records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909) — 199K records | 19th-century marriages | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196) — 3.2M images, browse-only | Wills and estates | Free |
| FamilySearch | Naturalization Records, 1790–1915 — 351 images, 15% indexed | Pre-1906 naturalizations | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Census for 1860–1900 | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Burial and grave information | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, labor news, legal notices | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Service and pension records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA | Naturalization, passenger lists, military records | Immigration and service records | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania in this period; all 3 are detailed above and this is the complete result set (no further pages).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Birth/death records from 1870, marriage licenses from 1885, deed books, probate files | In-person; some materials available on request |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) for many ethnic parishes | Contact diocesan archives directly |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records, industrial history collections, immigration records | In-person (https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/) |
| Rivers of Steel | Steel industry and labor records | Contact directly for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1813, local history collection, newspaper holdings | In-person and some digital |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records, 1798–1930 | In-person / NARA access |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State land office records, adjutant general records, factory inspector reports | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online

- **Allegheny County birth and death records (1870–1905):** County-level vital records before the statewide 1906 registration system are largely not digitized or indexed online; they must be requested at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Company employment records:** Carnegie Steel and related firm records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are not comprehensively indexed online.
- **Union membership lists:** No confirmed online access was found during this survey.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not available online.
- **Most Catholic parish registers:** Originals at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives are largely physical only; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch but are browse-only.

## Known record losses

No tool result during this survey stated that a specific Allegheny County or Pittsburgh record set was destroyed or lost. The absence of online digitization for some record classes (county vital records before 1906, company employment records) reflects a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. The fate of specific registers must be confirmed with the holding repositories.

## Research tips

- **For industrial workers, the city directory is your spine.** Pittsburgh directories from the 1870s–1900s list occupation and home address each year; use them to anchor a worker in time and place between censuses, then pivot to the census for family data. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses are your most information-rich census sources.** Both record occupation and birthplace of parents; 1900 also records immigration year — critical for immigrant steelworkers. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Match the ethnic background to the right Catholic parish.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Irish parishes each maintained separate registers; using the wrong parish will produce a dead end. Identify the specific ethnic parish (often indicated by the census or city directory neighborhood), then contact the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Naturalization records document arrival and birthplace.** Pre-1906 naturalizations at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia — these often state the immigrant's county and country of origin, which unlocks foreign research. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Vital records before 1906 were NOT statewide in Pennsylvania.** For births and deaths in the late 1800s, search both Allegheny County records (from 1870) and church registers; do not assume the statewide death certificate system covers these years. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content during this survey.** The Allegheny County page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and the Pennsylvania pages should be checked directly — they may carry additional detail not captured here.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No indexed population data was returned by tools; Pittsburgh was among the largest U.S. cities by 1900, with Allegheny County's population driven by the steel boom
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated from the 1870s onward; Carnegie Steel and related firms made Pittsburgh the center of American steel production, attracting massive immigrant labor flows (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants poured into the city and surrounding mill towns during the late 1800s
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (with numerous ethnic parishes organized by nationality), mainline Protestant; ethnic Catholic parishes were the primary record-keeping institutions for many immigrant families
- **Key historical events:** Steel industry boom of the 1870s–1900s drove massive immigration; the Homestead Strike (1892) is a notable event affecting labor records

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since its formation in 1788.
- The city of Allegheny (across the Ohio and Allegheny rivers from Pittsburgh) was a separate municipality until annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Records for residents of what is now Pittsburgh's North Side were created under "Allegheny city" jurisdictional headings before 1907 — a critical distinction when searching vital, court, and directory records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates:** Allegheny County recorded births and deaths at the **county level from 1870** — earlier than Pennsylvania's statewide mandate. Statewide civil registration began in **1906** for births and deaths. Marriage licenses at the county courthouse from **1885**. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records); [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **What exists:** County-level birth and death records 1870–1905 (at the Allegheny County courthouse); statewide death certificates 1906–1968 on FamilySearch (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed with images); county marriage licenses from 1885 (coll. 1921317, 524,189 records)
- **Where held:** County records at the Allegheny County courthouse; statewide death certificates at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration exists before 1870 at any level for Allegheny County; the statewide series begins only in 1906.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary source before 1870 and for many families between 1870 and 1906.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes: Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish, with registers from the 1840s onward); mainline Protestant. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Originals for many Catholic parishes are at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**; FamilySearch has microfilmed some registers. Identify the specific ethnic parish before searching.
- **Gaps:** Protestant parish coverage varies by congregation; surviving registers must be identified parish by parish. No comprehensive online index exists for Allegheny County parish registers.
- **Language:** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and German parishes often kept registers in their national language — these records require reading the original.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Records for Allegheny County survive from 1800. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are most valuable for steel-era workers: both record occupation and birthplace of parents; 1900 also records immigration year. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no regular state census during this period; tax assessment lists serve as intercensal substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census — the 1870 and 1880 rounds cover the early steel era.
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, letters of administration
- **Date range:** From colonial period; Allegheny County from 1788
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (courthouse); FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3,200,560 images but is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Search wills first; if none, look for administration records for the same estate.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's grants in 1681 onward. County deeds begin at Allegheny County's formation in 1788. ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax assessment lists
- **Date range:** County deeds from 1788; state land office records from 1681
- **Where held:** Deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds; state patents at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865), Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era), draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds service and pension records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has many indexed military records online; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive coverage of Pittsburgh-area cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries and church burial grounds; ethnic Catholic cemeteries often have burial registers at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily papers in the late 1800s. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pittsburgh newspapers; the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh also holds local papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news (especially Homestead Strike coverage), legal notices, naturalization announcements

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants arrived via East Coast ports (New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore); passenger lists are at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; naturalization petitions (pre-1906 at any court of record); Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia; FamilySearch has Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (1790–1915), 15% indexed, 351 images browsable.
- **Immigration to Pittsburgh's mills:** Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia document the massive immigration to the steel mills. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. The 1880 and 1900 censuses record immigration year, providing a cross-reference for family arrival windows.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property assessment lists, personal property lists
- **Date range:** County tax lists from 1788; Pennsylvania tax lists survive from the 1690s in some counties ([Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists serve as census substitutes between federal enumerations and document property ownership

### Other record types — industrial and occupational sources

This is the most distinctive record category for Pittsburgh in this period and deserves priority attention:

- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary records from Carnegie Steel and related firms survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel** archives. These are not comprehensively indexed — contact both repositories directly. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **Union membership lists:** Steelworkers' union records may survive at the United Steelworkers archives or the Heinz History Center; availability is fragmentary.
- **City directories:** Pittsburgh city directories begin in 1813 and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; directories from the 1870s–1900s list occupations and home addresses, making them an indispensable year-by-year tracking tool for steel-era workers. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published reports in the late 1800s that may name specific workers or list workforce demographics; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Federal census occupation columns:** Every federal census from 1870 to 1900 records occupation; "iron puddler," "steel roller," and similar entries identify steel-era workers specifically.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (coll. 2255317) — 4.2M records | Deaths from 1906 onward | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (coll. 1921317) — 524K records | Marriages from 1885 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957) — 312K records | Earlier marriage records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909) — 199K records | 19th-century marriages | Free |
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196) — 3.2M images, browse-only | Wills and estates | Free |
| FamilySearch | Naturalization Records, 1790–1915 — 351 images, 15% indexed | Pre-1906 naturalizations | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Census for 1860–1900 | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Burial and grave information | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, labor news, legal notices | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Service and pension records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA | Naturalization, passenger lists, military records | Immigration and service records | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes for Pennsylvania in this period; all 3 are detailed above and this is the complete result set (no further pages).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Birth/death records from 1870, marriage licenses from 1885, deed books, probate files | In-person; some materials available on request |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) for many ethnic parishes | Contact diocesan archives directly |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records, industrial history collections, immigration records | In-person (https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/) |
| Rivers of Steel | Steel industry and labor records | Contact directly for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1813, local history collection, newspaper holdings | In-person and some digital |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records, 1798–1930 | In-person / NARA access |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State land office records, adjutant general records, factory inspector reports | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online

- **Allegheny County birth and death records (1870–1905):** County-level vital records before the statewide 1906 registration system are largely not digitized or indexed online; they must be requested at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Company employment records:** Carnegie Steel and related firm records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are not comprehensively indexed online.
- **Union membership lists:** No confirmed online access was found during this survey.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not available online.
- **Most Catholic parish registers:** Originals at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives are largely physical only; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch but are browse-only.

## Known record losses

No tool result during this survey stated that a specific Allegheny County or Pittsburgh record set was destroyed or lost. The absence of online digitization for some record classes (county vital records before 1906, company employment records) reflects a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. The fate of specific registers must be confirmed with the holding repositories.

## Research tips

- **For industrial workers, the city directory is your spine.** Pittsburgh directories from the 1870s–1900s list occupation and home address each year; use them to anchor a worker in time and place between censuses, then pivot to the census for family data. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses are your most information-rich census sources.** Both record occupation and birthplace of parents; 1900 also records immigration year — critical for immigrant steelworkers. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Match the ethnic background to the right Catholic parish.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Irish parishes each maintained separate registers; using the wrong parish will produce a dead end. Identify the specific ethnic parish (often indicated by the census or city directory neighborhood), then contact the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Naturalization records document arrival and birthplace.** Pre-1906 naturalizations at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia — these often state the immigrant's county and country of origin, which unlocks foreign research. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Vital records before 1906 were NOT statewide in Pennsylvania.** For births and deaths in the late 1800s, search both Allegheny County records (from 1870) and church registers; do not assume the statewide death certificate system covers these years. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content during this survey.** The Allegheny County page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and the Pennsylvania pages should be checked directly — they may carry additional detail not captured here.
