# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia incorporated within it
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making it the largest city in the United States at the time; roughly 5,000 died in the 1793 epidemic (Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793)
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; mercantile, shipping, and artisan trades dominant
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English, German, Scots-Irish, with significant Quaker, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, and Catholic communities
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed, and others
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic of August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 people (one-tenth of the population) and caused thousands more to flee; this is the defining event for genealogical research in this period

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County and City boundaries were essentially coterminous for this period; no significant boundary changes affected the jurisdiction between 1780 and 1810.
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 later unified city and county, but that is outside the target window.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates" (collection 1255317) begins in 1906, confirming statewide registration began at the state level around that date. The wiki_search result states: "church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906" (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death, birth, or marriage certificates. Church registers and special epidemic documentation substitute entirely.
- **Where held:** No civil vital registration records exist for 1793 Philadelphia.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; Committee records; church marriage registers.

### Epidemic-specific records (1793)
These are the primary finding tools for the yellow fever period and have no equivalent in ordinary years:
- **Mathew Carey's account:** A published list of names of the dead compiled during and shortly after the epidemic. Held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Committee of Citizens records:** Minutes and reports of the citizen committee organized to respond to the epidemic document individuals aided, deceased, or relocated. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the emergency hospital that treated epidemic patients. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Access:** These are physical records at their holding repositories; digitization status was not confirmed by any tool in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, one of the most complete registers), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes', founded 1642), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Parish archives, denominational archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (indexes), and FamilySearch microfilm. FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800), image group 001188322, covering 145 images; it is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be browsed image by image.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki was unreachable during this survey, so a complete list of surviving registers cannot be confirmed from tool results. The wiki_search result names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as among the most complete for the epidemic period.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') registers may include Swedish or German passages in earlier volumes.
- **Note:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records); consult their published indexes before searching raw registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the closest enumeration before the epidemic and would show pre-epidemic household composition. The 1800 census shows survivors and family reconstitution after the epidemic. Both are name-indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania had no regular state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia tax records (see Tax records below) function as a quasi-census for property owners.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships (for orphaned children of epidemic victims)
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) covers this period; it holds 3,200,560 images but is browse-only (no index, no full-text search) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Register of Wills and Orphans' Court, Philadelphia City Archives. The 1793–1794 period saw a surge in probate filings due to epidemic deaths; the Orphans' Court records are especially important for identifying minor children left without parents.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch (collection 1999196); physical originals at Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary land grants under the Penn family; deed recording at the county level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property were unreachable during this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), tax records
- **Date range:** Deed books from colonial period through this window
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds, Philadelphia City Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) produced service records and pension files for veterans still living in Philadelphia in 1793. The War of 1812 (1812–1815) is at the edge of the target window.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (Fold3: https://www.fold3.com/; NARA: https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Mikveh Israel Cemetery (Jewish), and multiple other church burial grounds throughout the city. Epidemic burials in 1793 were sometimes in ad hoc locations outside normal church grounds due to the volume of deaths.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed headstone data for some Philadelphia cemeteries; coverage for 1793 is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches and their archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793, including the Pennsylvania Gazette and Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser. These carried death notices, estate notices, and legal announcements during and after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized holdings; Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania for physical copies and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, legal notices, and contemporary epidemic accounts naming individuals

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port of entry; passenger arrival records are relevant for newly arrived families.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are sparse); naturalization petitions filed in Philadelphia courts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, 1700–1900) may assist with immigrant family identification.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia tax assessments functioned as a quasi-census, listing heads of household, property descriptions, and taxable values
- **Date range:** Available from the colonial period; the 1793–1800 window is covered
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; some are microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1793 and surrounding years can show who was present in the city before the epidemic, who disappeared from the rolls (potential epidemic victims), and who appeared afterward (survivors, newcomers)

### Other record types
- **Orphans' Court:** A specific court handling estates of minors and incompetent persons; especially important for identifying children orphaned by the 1793 epidemic. Part of the broader probate jurisdiction.
- **Philadelphia City Archives:** Holds a wide range of civic records including almshouse registers, poor relief records, and mayoral correspondence — all of which document epidemic victims and survivors.
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania:** Holds manuscript collections, diaries, and published accounts documenting the epidemic. Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) is a key finding tool naming the dead.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312K indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 199K indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 browse-only images) | Probate surges after epidemic; church marriage indexes; Quaker records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 and 1800 federal censuses showing pre- and post-epidemic households | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Headstone transcriptions for Philadelphia church burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War pension files for veterans living in Philadelphia in 1793 | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records including naturalization petitions and passenger lists | Free/in-person |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | 1793 death notices, estate notices, epidemic-era newspaper accounts | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia in this period; it was the complete result set for the 1750–1830 window at the county level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Civic records, Committee of Citizens epidemic records, Bush Hill hospital records, Orphans' Court, tax records, deed books | In-person; inquire about reproduction services |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Mathew Carey's account, manuscript collections, diaries, church record microfilm | In-person; some digitized collections via HSP website |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person / published volumes / Ancestry partnership |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism/marriage/burial registers | Contact each church or denomination directly |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level military and administrative records | In-person / mail requests |

## Records NOT online
- Mathew Carey's list of epidemic dead (physical at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; digitization status not confirmed by tools)
- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports (physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP)
- Bush Hill hospital records (physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP)
- Philadelphia tax assessment rolls for 1793 (some microfilmed; check FamilySearch Catalog)
- Most individual church registers from this period (exceptions: some are microfilmed; Quaker minutes are digitized browse-only)
- Orphans' Court records for the 1793–1794 surge period (part of probate collection 1999196, browse-only)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Philadelphia record set was destroyed for the 1793 period. The generic nature of the wiki-query-api responses means that any locally known losses were not surfaced. Contact the Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania directly to confirm the survival status of specific record series.

- **Start with the epidemic finding tools before church registers.** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) and the Committee of Citizens records name many of the dead directly and are faster to search than individual church burial registers. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Church records are the vital record substitute for all of 1793.** No civil registration existed; every baptism, marriage, and burial in this period is in a church register. Identify your ancestor's denomination before searching. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Search probate immediately after identifying a death.** The 1793–1794 Orphans' Court and Register of Wills dockets are dense with epidemic-related filings, often naming children, spouses, and creditors. Use FamilySearch collection 1999196 (browse-only) or visit the Philadelphia City Archives in person.

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia in this period; it was the complete result set for the 1750–1830 window at the county level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Civic records, Committee of Citizens epidemic records, Bush Hill hospital records, Orphans' Court, tax records, deed books | In-person; inquire about reproduction services |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Mathew Carey's account, manuscript collections, diaries, church record microfilm | In-person; some digitized collections via HSP website |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person / published volumes / Ancestry partnership |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism/marriage/burial registers | Contact each church or denomination directly |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level military and administrative records | In-person / mail requests |

## Records NOT online
- Mathew Carey's list of epidemic dead (physical at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; digitization status not confirmed by tools)
- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports (physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP)
- Bush Hill hospital records (physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP)
- Philadelphia tax assessment rolls for 1793 (some microfilmed; check FamilySearch Catalog)
- Most individual church registers from this period (exceptions: some are microfilmed; Quaker minutes are digitized browse-only)
- Orphans' Court records for the 1793–1794 surge period (part of probate collection 1999196, browse-only)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Philadelphia record set was destroyed for the 1793 period. The generic nature of the wiki-query-api responses means that any locally known losses were not surfaced. Contact the Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania directly to confirm the survival status of specific record series.

## Research tips
- **Start with the epidemic finding tools before church registers.** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) and the Committee of Citizens records name many of the dead directly and are faster to search than individual church burial registers. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Church records are the vital record substitute for all of 1793.** No civil registration existed; every baptism, marriage, and burial in this period is in a church register. Identify your ancestor's denomination before searching. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Search probate immediately after identifying a death.** The 1793–1794 Orphans' Court and Register of Wills dockets are dense with epidemic-related filings, often naming children, spouses, and creditors. Use FamilySearch collection 1999196 (browse-only) or visit the Philadelphia City Archives in person.
- **Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** Households that appear in 1790 but are absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic losses or the flight from the city. The difference between the two enumerations is a primary research tool for this period.
- **Tax assessment rolls substitute for absent census years.** Annual Philadelphia tax lists for 1791–1799 can track household heads year by year through the epidemic period and confirm who survived or relocated.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki was unreachable for all specific Philadelphia and Pennsylvania pages during this survey.** The pages at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy and related articles may contain additional guidance — visit them directly before relying on this guide's gaps as confirmed absences.

Locality guide **loc_001** is now saved to your project. Here's what it covers:

---

## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871: Records & Repositories

### The Core Challenge
The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it most pre-1871 civil records — deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers. This means that FamilySearch's indexed collections for Cook County births, deaths, and marriages all begin in 1871, not because civil registration started then, but because earlier records were lost.

---

### Best Pre-Fire Substitutes

| Source | Why It Survived | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|
| **1870 Federal Census** | Originals were in Washington, D.C., not the courthouse | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **City Directories (1840s onward)** | Held at the Newberry Library | Newberry Library, Chicago |
| **Chicago Title & Trust Co. insurance records** | Pre-fire property evidence | Chicago History Museum (not online) |
| **Church registers outside the burn zone** | Some parishes were spared | Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives |

---

### Post-Fire Recovery Records

- **Burnt Record Act of 1872**: Required landowners to re-register their deeds. FamilySearch has digitized these re-recordings (1871–1880, ~41% name-indexed) — a key source for tracing property and residence.

---

### FamilySearch Indexed Collections (Cook County)

| Collection | Records | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Cook County Church Records | ~285,000 | 1833–1925 |
| Cook County Births | ~1.45 million | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Deaths | ~980,000 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriages | ~620,000 | 1871–1920 |

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the 1870 federal census** to establish the family before the fire.
2. **Search post-fire vital records** (births, deaths, marriages) on FamilySearch for the specific family.
3. **Check Newberry Library city directories** to trace residence and occupation.
4. **If property is relevant**, search the Burnt Record Act re-recordings on FamilySearch.
5. **For Catholic families**, contact the Archdiocese of Chicago's Bernardin Archives for surviving parish registers.

> **Note:** Illinois-specific vital registration start dates could not be confirmed from tool results during this survey — verify directly on the FamilySearch Wiki.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (statehood 1818)
- **Population during period:** Population figures could not be confirmed by the place_population tool for this survey.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, rail hub, lumber, manufacturing, commerce — a rapidly growing immigrant industrial city
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrant communities by the 1870s; the fire's displacement exacerbated record gaps for these groups
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations, and many others reflecting the city's immigrant population
- **Key historical events:** Great Fire of October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, displaced more than 100,000 residents, and wiped out most pre-1871 civil and many church records (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the 1850–1900 period; Chicago's city limits expanded through annexation but records remained at the county level
- No parent-jurisdiction succession issues for this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and no specific registration start dates could be confirmed from it. The FamilySearch collections for Cook County begin in 1871 for births (collection 2024189), deaths (collection 1913456), and marriages (collection 1756321) — consistent with the destruction of pre-fire records.
- **What exists:** Birth certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records, collection 2024189); death records 1871–1947 (980,000 records, collection 1913456); marriage records 1871–1920 (620,000 records, collection 1756321) — all on FamilySearch
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office holds originals; FamilySearch has indexed digital collections
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil vital records were largely destroyed in the Great Fire; statewide Illinois registration dates were not confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, city directories, federal census, newspaper notices, insurance records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish, and many ethnic-community churches; FamilySearch collection 1803978 covers Cook County Chicago church records 1833–1925 (285,000 records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic records at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives; other denominations at their respective archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire registers (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Gaps:** Many church registers in the fire zone were destroyed in October 1871; surviving pre-fire registers are those held by parishes outside the burn area or churches that subsequently reconstructed records
- **Language:** Most records in English; German, Polish, and other immigrant-community languages appear in ethnic parish registers

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all available; critically, the 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the originals were in Washington, D.C. — this is the primary source for identifying families present before the fire (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **State/provincial census:** Illinois state censuses were taken in intercensal years; this survey did not confirm their survival or digitization from tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch; the 1870 is especially important as a pre-fire anchor

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, naturalizations
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate and court records were largely destroyed; FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes for Chicago — volume 009982110 covers reconstructed pre-fire Cook County Court Records 1865–1871 (38 images, **browse-only**, 0% name-indexed, must be browsed image by image) and volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (112 images, 41% name-indexed — indexed + images)
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County records post-1871; Cook County courthouse holds later originals
- **Note on naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; post-fire Cook County court records at IRAD-NEIU should be searched for immigrant families

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Township and range (rectangular survey — Illinois is a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Land and Property page was not retrieved during this survey; federal land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, mortgages; crucially, reconstructed deeds filed under the Burnt Record Act (1872), which required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire
- **Date range:** Post-fire deed re-registrations begin 1872; pre-fire deeds were largely destroyed
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (41% indexed)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registration, bounty land warrants; Civil War records are especially relevant for men of enlistment age in the 1860s
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) at https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ provides online access to many military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Chicago has multiple large cemeteries serving immigrant communities; specific names and denominational affiliations were not confirmed by tool results in this survey
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ covers many Cook County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by individual cemeteries or the Chicago History Museum

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had multiple daily newspapers during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com at https://www.newspapers.com/ provides online access to historical Chicago newspapers; the Newberry Library holds physical microfilm
- **Content value:** Fire-era news (survivor lists, missing persons notices, relief rolls), obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices — fire-era newspaper coverage is a primary substitute for destroyed vital records

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago was an inland destination; most immigrants arrived through East Coast ports (New York, Baltimore, Boston) or Great Lakes ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906 in any court of record, post-1906 through the INS); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization files at IRAD-NEIU for Cook County courts
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed; post-fire records begin with the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872)
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor's records; this survey did not confirm online availability
- **Substitute value:** Post-fire tax records can substitute for missing property documentation; pre-fire city directories serve as the primary substitute for missing census or tax years before 1871

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — these are a critical pre-fire substitute, naming residents by address and occupation (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a key pre-fire substitute source for property ownership and family information (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)
- **Relief records:** Post-fire relief organizations documented displaced families; the Chicago History Museum may hold some of these records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (statehood 1818)
- **Population during period:** Population figures could not be confirmed by the place_population tool for this survey.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, rail hub, lumber, manufacturing, commerce — a rapidly growing immigrant industrial city
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrant communities by the 1870s; the fire's displacement exacerbated record gaps for these groups
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations, and many others reflecting the city's immigrant population
- **Key historical events:** Great Fire of October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, displaced more than 100,000 residents, and wiped out most pre-1871 civil and many church records (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the 1850–1900 period; Chicago's city limits expanded through annexation but records remained at the county level
- No parent-jurisdiction succession issues for this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and no specific registration start dates could be confirmed from it. The FamilySearch collections for Cook County begin in 1871 for births (collection 2024189), deaths (collection 1913456), and marriages (collection 1756321) — consistent with the destruction of pre-fire records.
- **What exists:** Birth certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records, collection 2024189); death records 1871–1947 (980,000 records, collection 1913456); marriage records 1871–1920 (620,000 records, collection 1756321) — all on FamilySearch
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office holds originals; FamilySearch has indexed digital collections
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil vital records were largely destroyed in the Great Fire; statewide Illinois registration dates were not confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, city directories, federal census, newspaper notices, insurance records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish, and many ethnic-community churches; FamilySearch collection 1803978 covers Cook County Chicago church records 1833–1925 (285,000 records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic records at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives; other denominations at their respective archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire registers (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Gaps:** Many church registers in the fire zone were destroyed in October 1871; surviving pre-fire registers are those held by parishes outside the burn area or churches that subsequently reconstructed records
- **Language:** Most records in English; German, Polish, and other immigrant-community languages appear in ethnic parish registers

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all available; critically, the 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the originals were in Washington, D.C. — this is the primary source for identifying families present before the fire (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **State/provincial census:** Illinois state censuses were taken in intercensal years; this survey did not confirm their survival or digitization from tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch; the 1870 is especially important as a pre-fire anchor

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, naturalizations
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate and court records were largely destroyed; FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes for Chicago — volume 009982110 covers reconstructed pre-fire Cook County Court Records 1865–1871 (38 images, **browse-only**, 0% name-indexed, must be browsed image by image) and volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (112 images, 41% name-indexed — indexed + images)
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County records post-1871; Cook County courthouse holds later originals
- **Note on naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; post-fire Cook County court records at IRAD-NEIU should be searched for immigrant families

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Township and range (rectangular survey — Illinois is a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Land and Property page was not retrieved during this survey; federal land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, mortgages; crucially, reconstructed deeds filed under the Burnt Record Act (1872), which required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire
- **Date range:** Post-fire deed re-registrations begin 1872; pre-fire deeds were largely destroyed
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (41% indexed)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registration, bounty land warrants; Civil War records are especially relevant for men of enlistment age in the 1860s
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) at https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ provides online access to many military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Chicago has multiple large cemeteries serving immigrant communities; specific names and denominational affiliations were not confirmed by tool results in this survey
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ covers many Cook County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by individual cemeteries or the Chicago History Museum

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had multiple daily newspapers during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com at https://www.newspapers.com/ provides online access to historical Chicago newspapers; the Newberry Library holds physical microfilm
- **Content value:** Fire-era news (survivor lists, missing persons notices, relief rolls), obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices — fire-era newspaper coverage is a primary substitute for destroyed vital records

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago was an inland destination; most immigrants arrived through East Coast ports (New York, Baltimore, Boston) or Great Lakes ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906 in any court of record, post-1906 through the INS); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization files at IRAD-NEIU for Cook County courts
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed; post-fire records begin with the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872)
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor's records; this survey did not confirm online availability
- **Substitute value:** Post-fire tax records can substitute for missing property documentation; pre-fire city directories serve as the primary substitute for missing census or tax years before 1871

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — these are a critical pre-fire substitute, naming residents by address and occupation (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)

- **Relief records:** Post-fire relief organizations documented displaced families; the Chicago History Museum may hold some of these records

Researching families in Louisiana during the 1700s means working in a colonial era that had **no civil registration at all**. The territory was French from 1699 to 1762, then Spanish until the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. During that entire period, the Catholic Church — the only legally recognized church under the colonial *Code Noir* — was the keeper of all vital records: baptisms, marriages, and burials.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was claimed for France in 1682 by La Salle; New Orleans was founded in 1718. France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain administered the colony until retroceding it to France in 1800; the United States acquired it in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of the Superior Council and Catholic diocese)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French colonial empire); Province of Louisiana under Spanish rule after 1762
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by this survey's tools; the colony had a small European settler population concentrated around New Orleans, with a large enslaved African population.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco); fur trade; river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Acadian refugees (from 1755 onward), Spanish colonial administrators, enslaved Africans, free persons of color, and Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church exclusively (the only legally recognized church under the Code Noir in French Louisiana)
- **Key historical events:** Code Noir (1724) required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons; Acadian expulsion and resettlement (1755–1769); Spanish assumption of control (effective 1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

## Boundary changes
- 1699–1762: Entire territory under French colonial rule (Superior Council at New Orleans)
- 1762: France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau); eastern Louisiana to Britain
- 1769: Spanish effective governance began under Governor Alejandro O'Reilly
- 1800–1803: Secretly retroceded to France; sold to the United States 1803
- Records during the Spanish colonial period (1769–1803) are often still written in French but were administered through Spanish legal structures; both French and Spanish record series must be searched.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the colonial period (1700s). The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and does not state a civil-registration start date for Louisiana; that date cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results.
- **What exists:** Catholic Church sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) served as the de facto vital records for all free colonists and, under the Code Noir, for enslaved persons. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720 (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Where held:** Originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral. FamilySearch holds a digitized but browse-only volume of Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 (image group 004330991, 264 images, French/Spanish, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable). FamilySearch indexed collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) also covers this period.
- **Gaps:** Records predating 1720 are extremely sparse; records from parishes outside New Orleans may survive only in physical form at individual church archives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial records (Superior Council), estate inventories, and colonial census rolls at ANOM.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic Church exclusively (the Code Noir prohibited any other public religious practice). Acadian Catholic communities arrived from 1755 onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals). FamilySearch holds two digitized but browse-only volumes: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans (1720–1803, image group 004330991, 264 images) and French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records (1699–1769, image group 004330992, 149 images). Both are in French and Spanish and must be browsed image-by-image with no name index.
- **Language:** French (1699–1762 period) and French/Spanish (Spanish colonial period 1762–1803). Researchers must be able to read these languages.
- **Gaps:** No surviving parish registers from before 1720 were confirmed by this survey's tools. Rural parishes outside New Orleans may have only physical records.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** No federal census existed during the colonial period. The French colonial administration conducted periodic census rolls (recensements); these are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Post-statehood federal census:** The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 (after the Louisiana Purchase, 1803), outside the 1700s target window.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM are physical records; contact ANOM directly or use their online catalog.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, administration proceedings, guardianships — all processed through the Superior Council (the colonial court of record).
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, indexed, with images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) covers the colonial period from 1756.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds original Superior Council records; some are partially digitized. FamilySearch collection 2078341 provides indexed access from 1756.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents), inherited by Spanish administration; not the American rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French concessions and Spanish land grants. Colonial-era land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgages, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s onward at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — one of the oldest continuous notarial offices in North America (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access, in-person). Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge. FamilySearch volume 004330992 (French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, 1699–1769, 149 images, browse-only, French).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763), Spanish colonial militia service (after 1769), American Revolution (some Louisiana militia involvement).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls and service records. This survey did not confirm digitized online access to colonial-era Louisiana military records.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) for the French colonial period; Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for the Spanish colonial period; Louisiana Historical Center for some derivative copies. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds U.S. military records but would not cover French/Spanish colonial service.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial burials:** Burial records for the colonial period are found in Catholic sacramental registers (burials section). St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, est. 1789) is the oldest surviving above-ground cemetery; records before 1789 are in church burial registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Louisiana cemeteries but colonial-era grave markers are largely not transcribed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records (where they survive) are at individual cemeteries or church archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Colonial papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, began in 1794 (late Spanish colonial period). No colonial newspapers from earlier in the 1700s were confirmed by this survey's tools.
- **Where held:** Historic New Orleans Collection and Louisiana State Library hold early newspaper microfilm.
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate sale announcements, and legal notices appear in late-colonial-era issues.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant movements:** French settlers from France, Canada (Acadians from 1755 onward), Caribbean (Saint-Domingue); enslaved Africans via the Atlantic slave trade.
- **Record types:** No formal immigration or passenger-list system existed in the colonial era. Ship passenger and cargo lists from the Superior Council records (Louisiana Historical Center; FamilySearch volume 004330992, browse-only) are the nearest equivalent. Acadian exile and resettlement records are at ANOM and in published works.
- **Naturalization:** No federal naturalization process applied during the French/Spanish colonial period.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger and cargo records are in French or Spanish and must be read in the original language.

### Tax records
- **Types:** No formal county-level property tax series existed in the French colonial era. Colonial census rolls (at ANOM) served some of the same enumerative function.
- **Post-statehood:** Louisiana parish tax records begin after 1803 and are outside the 1700s target window.

### Other record types
- **Enslaved-person records:** The Code Noir (1724) required baptism of enslaved persons, so they appear in Catholic sacramental registers. Estate inventories (in probate records) also enumerate enslaved people by name, age, and sometimes origin — a critical source for researching enslaved ancestors.
- **Notarial records:** Marriage contracts, property settlements, apprenticeships, and manumissions (freedom papers) are in notarial records at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center and in FamilySearch volume 004330992 (browse-only, French).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | Indexed baptisms, marriages, burials from 1718 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | Estate inventories, wills, court proceedings from 1756 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 |
| FamilySearch (image group 004330991) | Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 (264 images, browse-only) | Browse-only church registers in French/Spanish not in the indexed collection | Free — browse-only, no name index |
| FamilySearch (image group 004330992) | French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, 1699–1769 (149 images, browse-only) | Notarial acts, land grants, estate records, colonial-era contracts | Free — browse-only, no name index |
| NARA | National Archives | Post-1803 federal and territorial records | https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700–1800, and both are detailed above — these are the complete results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Original Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories); partially digitized | In-person / contact Louisiana State Museum |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts, marriage settlements, wills, property transactions from 1730s onward | In-person public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls | In-person / online catalog at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative and military records (1769–1803) | In-person / PARES online portal |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives / St. Louis Cathedral | Original sacramental registers from 1720 | Contact archives directly |
| Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / contact office |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial administrative correspondence and census rolls (at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence)
- Spanish colonial administrative and military records (Archivo General de Indias, Seville)
- Sacramental registers from parishes outside New Orleans — likely physical only at individual church or diocesan archives
- New Orleans Notarial Archives records beyond those partially included in FamilySearch volume 004330992

## Known record losses
No tool result returned by this survey specifically identified destroyed or lost record series for colonial Louisiana. The absence of surviving sacramental registers from before 1720 is a coverage gap — this survey cannot confirm whether records from before 1720 were destroyed or simply never created in a surviving form. Researchers should contact the Louisiana Historical Center and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives to determine the survival status of specific record sets.

## Research tips
- **Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital records for the colonial period.** Civil registration did not exist. All baptisms, marriages, and burials of free colonists — and, under the Code Noir, of enslaved persons — were recorded by the Catholic Church. Begin here before looking elsewhere. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **The Superior Council records are the colonial court of record.** Land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories passed through the Superior Council. These records are at the Louisiana Historical Center and partially accessible via FamilySearch image group 004330992 (browse-only, French). (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Records are in French and Spanish and must be read in the original language.** Both FamilySearch volumes are in French and Spanish. The transition to Spanish administration (effective 1769) did not immediately convert all records to Spanish; French continued in use. Use a translator or seek published transcriptions if needed.
- **The colonial period splits across two colonial powers.** The French period covers 1699–1762; the Spanish period 1762–1803. Records from each period may be in different repositories — ANOM (France) for the French period, Archivo General de Indias (Spain) for the Spanish period. Search both when researching families who lived through the transition.
- **The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold records from the 1730s.** Marriage contracts, property settlements, and manumissions (freedom documents) may name family members not found in church records. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **The Code Noir required baptism of enslaved persons.** This means enslaved individuals appear in Catholic sacramental registers. Estate inventories in probate records also enumerate enslaved people by name and sometimes age or origin, making probate records a critical source for researching enslaved ancestors.

- **Relevant movements:** French settlers from France, Canada (Acadians from 1755 onward), Caribbean (Saint-Domingue); enslaved Africans via the Atlantic slave trade.
- **Record types:** No formal immigration or passenger-list system existed in the colonial era. Ship passenger and cargo lists from the Superior Council records (Louisiana Historical Center; FamilySearch volume 004330992, browse-only) are the nearest equivalent. Acadian exile and resettlement records are at ANOM and in published works.
- **Naturalization:** No federal naturalization process applied during the French/Spanish colonial period.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger and cargo records are in French or Spanish and must be read in the original language.

### Tax records
- **Types:** No formal county-level property tax series existed in the French colonial era. Colonial census rolls (at ANOM) served some of the same enumerative function.
- **Post-statehood:** Louisiana parish tax records begin after 1803 and are outside the 1700s target window.

### Other record types
- **Enslaved-person records:** The Code Noir (1724) required baptism of enslaved persons, so they appear in Catholic sacramental registers. Estate inventories (in probate records) also enumerate enslaved people by name, age, and sometimes origin — a critical source for researching enslaved ancestors.
- **Notarial records:** Marriage contracts, property settlements, apprenticeships, and manumissions (freedom papers) are in notarial records at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center and in FamilySearch volume 004330992 (browse-only, French).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | Indexed baptisms, marriages, burials from 1718 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905 |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | Estate inventories, wills, court proceedings from 1756 | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 |
| FamilySearch (image group 004330991) | Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 (264 images, browse-only) | Browse-only church registers in French/Spanish not in the indexed collection | Free — browse-only, no name index |
| FamilySearch (image group 004330992) | French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, 1699–1769 (149 images, browse-only) | Notarial acts, land grants, estate records, colonial-era contracts | Free — browse-only, no name index |
| NARA | National Archives | Post-1803 federal and territorial records | https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700–1800, and both are detailed above — these are the complete results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Original Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories); partially digitized | In-person / contact Louisiana State Museum |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts, marriage settlements, wills, property transactions from 1730s onward | In-person public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls | In-person / online catalog at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative and military records (1769–1803) | In-person / PARES online portal |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives / St. Louis Cathedral | Original sacramental registers from 1720 | Contact archives directly |
| Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / contact office |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial administrative correspondence and census rolls (at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence)
- Spanish colonial administrative and military records (Archivo General de Indias, Seville)
- Sacramental registers from parishes outside New Orleans — likely physical only at individual church or diocesan archives
- New Orleans Notarial Archives records beyond those partially included in FamilySearch volume 004330992

## Known record losses
No tool result returned by this survey specifically identified destroyed or lost record series for colonial Louisiana. The absence of surviving sacramental registers from before 1720 is a coverage gap — this survey cannot confirm whether records from before 1720 were destroyed or simply never created in a surviving form. Researchers should contact the Louisiana Historical Center and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives to determine the survival status of specific record sets.

## Research tips
- **Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital records for the colonial period.** Civil registration did not exist. All baptisms, marriages, and burials of free colonists — and, under the Code Noir, of enslaved persons — were recorded by the Catholic Church. Begin here before looking elsewhere. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **The Superior Council records are the colonial court of record.** Land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories passed through the Superior Council. These records are at the Louisiana Historical Center and partially accessible via FamilySearch image group 004330992 (browse-only, French). (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Records are in French and Spanish and must be read in the original language.** Both FamilySearch volumes are in French and Spanish. The transition to Spanish administration (effective 1769) did not immediately convert all records to Spanish; French continued in use. Use a translator or seek published transcriptions if needed.
- **The colonial period splits across two colonial powers.** The French period covers 1699–1762; the Spanish period 1762–1803. Records from each period may be in different repositories — ANOM (France) for the French period, Archivo General de Indias (Spain) for the Spanish period. Search both when researching families who lived through the transition.
- **The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold records from the 1730s.** Marriage contracts, property settlements, and manumissions (freedom documents) may name family members not found in church records. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **The Code Noir required baptism of enslaved persons.** This means enslaved individuals appear in Catholic sacramental registers. Estate inventories in probate records also enumerate enslaved people by name and sometimes age or origin, making probate records a critical source for researching enslaved ancestors.

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Guide (1850–1910)

**Focus county:** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), the heart of Pennsylvania's anthracite region. The same record types apply to neighboring **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland** counties, each of which would need its own survey if research there is planned.

---

### Coal-Industry–Specific Records
These are the most distinctive records for mining families:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County (1870–1900)** — 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch.
- **State Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870)** — published reports name every fatal accident victim with age, nationality, and cause of death. Invaluable for mining families.

---

### Vital Records
- **Pennsylvania death certificates** begin in 1906 on FamilySearch. For deaths before that date, church registers are the primary source.
- **Births and marriages** before state registration must be traced through **church baptismal and marriage registers**.
- Because mining communities organized around ethnic parishes, you must identify the correct denomination first:
  - Irish Catholic
  - Welsh Congregational
  - Polish Catholic
  - Lithuanian Catholic
  - (and other immigrant communities)

---

### Naturalization Records
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (not NARA), because miners naturalized in local courts of record before the 1906 federal reform.

---

### Census Records
- Federal census records (1850–1910) are available through FamilySearch and other repositories and are foundational for locating mining households, ages, birthplaces, and neighbors.

---

### Key Repositories
| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Mine employment cards, death certificates (1906+), census, some church records |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Naturalization records, state-level records |
| **Local county courthouses** | Pre-1906 vital records, deeds, probate |
| **Ethnic/denominational church archives** | Baptisms, marriages, burials for immigrant parishes |

---

### Important Caveat
During this survey, FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania (Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land, and Probate) returned only generic content — so Pennsylvania-specific registration start dates could not be confirmed from tool results. **Visit those wiki pages directly** before concluding that a record series does not exist for a given period.

---

### Suggested Next Step
Run a **research plan** for the specific county where your ancestor lived, using this guide as the foundation to map searches for parentage, immigration origin, or other open questions.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1850–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed in this survey's tool results
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned during this survey (place_population returned no data)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish Catholic, Welsh, Polish, and Lithuanian immigrant communities documented in ethnic parishes ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic
- **Key historical events:** State Mine Inspector annual reports published from 1870; United Mine Workers of America founded 1890

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811; boundaries appear stable through the target period
- Neighboring Lackawanna County separated from Luzerne County around 1878 — the volume_search returned Lackawanna volumes beginning that year; events in that area before 1878 were recorded under Luzerne County

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and gave no Pennsylvania-specific vital registration start dates with levels. FamilySearch collection 2255317 ("Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968") begins in 1906, but no wiki page confirmed when statewide death registration was required.
- **What exists:** Death certificates from 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images); county marriages from 1885 (collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records); civil marriages from 1677 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records); compiled marriage index 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images). No indexed statewide birth certificate collection for the late 1800s was returned by this survey.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch for collections above; county courthouse for original registers
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth certificate collection for births before 1906 was returned; for births, church baptismal registers are the primary alternative
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; Mine Inspector reports for deaths from mining accidents

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic — each served specific mining communities ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm; identifying the congregation is essential before searching, as registers are organized by parish, not county
- **Gaps:** No confirmed digitized Schuylkill County church record collection was returned by this survey (one entry in the collections_search was explicitly labeled a synthetic test fixture and is excluded from this guide)
- **Language:** Records of Polish and Lithuanian parishes will be in those languages

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Decennial enumerations 1850–1910 all cover this period; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/). The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules list occupation as "miner" for coal mining families ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** The generic wiki content mentions mortality schedules recording deaths in the year preceding each census; Pennsylvania-specific coverage was not confirmed in this survey
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not hold a state census; none returned for this period
- **Access:** Indexed and searchable via Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Date range:** Collection 1999196 ("Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994") covers this period
- **Access:** Browse-only images (3,200,560 images; 0% name-indexed) — must be browsed image by image with no search capability
- **Where held:** FamilySearch for browse-only images; Schuylkill County Courthouse for originals

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds state (not rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** No Pennsylvania-specific land office details were confirmed by this survey's wiki pages
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** County courthouse for deed books; Pennsylvania State Archives for earlier records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 for digitized military records (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is available for Schuylkill County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Historical Society of Schuylkill County may hold transcriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No specific Schuylkill County newspaper titles or date ranges were confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; local library or historical society for microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York — primary arrival ports for Irish and Eastern European miners ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (at NARA); naturalization records; Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for passenger lists; Pennsylvania State Archives for Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property
- **Where held:** County courthouse, Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years

### Other record types — coal mining specific
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900):** Image group 002240015; 410 images; 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — the most accessible mining-specific digitized source for this county
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870–1895):** Image group 002240016; 287 images; browse-only — no name index
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878–1900):** Image group 002240017; 199 images; browse-only
- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870):** State-published reports listing fatal accident victims by name, age, nationality, and cause of death; held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA membership rolls (from 1890):** United Mine Workers of America grievance files and membership rolls; held at local historical societies

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 2255317 (Death Certs, 1906-1968, 4.2M records); 1921317 (County Marriages, 1885-1950, 524K records); 1999196 (Probate Records, 1683-1994, browse-only); 1571957 (Civil Marriages, 1677-1950); 1502909 (Compiled Marriages index, 1700-1900) | Vital records, probate | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records not name-indexed on FamilySearch | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records not in vital record series | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, accident notices absent from vital records before 1906 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service records for Civil War and Spanish-American War | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, federal naturalization post-1906 | Free/In-person |

Here is the locality guide for early Massachusetts Puritan research:

---

**Massachusetts, 1620–1700: Locality Research Guide** *(saved as loc_001)*

**Two Separate Colonies**
This period covers two distinct jurisdictions — **Plymouth Colony** (1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1630) — which remained separate until they merged in 1691. Their records are published and indexed independently, so it's important to know which colony your ancestor settled in.

**Key Record Types**

- **Town Vital Records** — Births, marriages, and deaths were required at the town level from **1639** onward. These are the most consistently surviving records for this era.
- **Congregational Church Registers** — Baptisms, memberships, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings. These are often the *only* records predating 1639, making them critical for the earliest settlers.
- **Probate Records** — Survive from the 1630s onward, held at county probate courts.
- **Deed and Land Proprietors' Records** — Held at county registries; important for tracing land transactions and family relationships.

**FamilySearch Collections (Confirmed)**
FamilySearch holds:
- Indexed collections for town vital records, church records, and probate records
- Two digitized but unindexed volumes:
  - Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (browse image by image)
  - Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, 1630–1700 (full-text searchable but not name-indexed)
