added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Plymouth Colony founded 1620 and operated separately until 1691, when both were merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Governor John Winthrop led approximately 20,000 settlers in the Great Migration between 1630 and 1640 (per Wikipedia); no colonial census exists to give a precise figure for 1700.
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, lumber, coastal trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; indigenous Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Narragansett nations throughout the region
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) established church; small Quaker meetings after 1656; Anglican minority
- **Key historical events:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678) caused widespread destruction of towns and loss of records across central and western Massachusetts

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) operated as a wholly separate colony with its own government, courts, and vital-record system. Its records are indexed and published separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records.
- In 1691, Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter, unifying the record-keeping systems.
- For ancestors in Plymouth Colony towns (Plymouth, Duxbury, Barnstable, Marshfield, etc.) before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records as a separate research trail from Massachusetts Bay records.
- Massachusetts Bay County formation began in 1643 with Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk Counties. Land deeds and probate records follow county lines from that date; for events before 1643, the Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records are the governing source.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town level — the Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, one of the earliest civil vital-record mandates in North America (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Statewide (state-level) registration did not begin until 1842. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page was not accessible during this survey to confirm additional registration-level detail.
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from the 1630s onward, in varying completeness. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covers this period and is searchable online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550.
- **Gaps:** King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed or damaged records in many towns; some towns did not begin recording until years after the 1639 mandate; early entries are sparse.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established and dominant church. Small Quaker meetings emerged after 1656. Anglican presence was minimal before 1700.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments), and burial records.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. Originals are held by surviving congregations, with many deposited at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston), NEHGS, and local historical societies. Many have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy.
- **Gaps:** Not all early congregations kept systematic registers; some were lost in King Philip's War.
- **Language:** English.

One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612045, 121 images) covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700; it is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — it cannot be searched by name and must be accessed via text search.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Begins in 1790 — entirely outside this period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No systematic colonial census survives for Massachusetts Bay for 1620–1700. Town meeting records, tax lists (town rates), and militia muster rolls serve as partial substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Proprietors' lists in town records enumerate landowning householders by name.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships.
- **Date range:** From 1635 for Massachusetts Bay counties; Plymouth Colony probate from the 1630s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901. Originals held at county probate courts and Massachusetts Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Probate Records page was not accessible during this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors distributed land within each town; county registries of deeds recorded conveyances from the 1630s. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page was not accessible during this survey to confirm the granting office.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, grants, mortgages.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives. One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612044, 188 images) covers town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 — browse-only images, not name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678). No federal military records exist for this period.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, pay lists, and council-of-war proceedings held in the Massachusetts Archives. Published transcriptions appear in the Massachusetts Historical Society Collections series.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Historical Society.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burying grounds associated with Congregational meeting houses (e.g., King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1630; Granary Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1660).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many early Massachusetts cemeteries with transcribed inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the 17th century; gravestone inscriptions are frequently the only direct evidence of burial.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No sustained newspaper existed in Massachusetts before 1704 (Boston News-Letter). Newspapers are essentially unavailable as a source for 1620–1700.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of entry.
- **Record types:** English port departure records (held in England); ship passenger lists reconstructed by historians. The Great Migration study (NEHGS) documents known arrivals 1620–1643 from multiple sources.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) covers only 1820–1891 and does not apply to the 1620–1700 period. For 17th-century arrivals, use the Great Migration study volumes (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS) and English records (State Papers, port books) available through Ancestry and FindMyPast.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger lists are reconstructed from English and colonial sources, not from systematic American manifests (which did not exist). The full manifest of a ship record names all passengers including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rates (property and poll taxes) recorded in town meeting records.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Massachusetts Archives; some published in historical society series.
- **Substitute value:** A name in town rates confirms presence in the community at a specific date, substituting for census in the colonial period.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Minutes name every male taxpayer and record votes on local affairs, road maintenance, care of the poor, and land allotments — an indispensable source for colonial-period research.
- **Colony/General Court records:** The Massachusetts Bay General Court records (Massachusetts Archives) document laws, petitions, land grants, and judicial proceedings from the 1630s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (1678901) | Town-level vital, church, and probate records 1620–1700 | Free; https://www.familysearch.org |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Gravestone inscriptions where no burial register survives | Free; https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| NARA | General federal holdings | Federal records (mostly post-1700 for this region) | Free online / in-person; https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620–1700 — this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). Both are browse-only or full-text searchable but not name-indexed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, General Court records, colonial court records, vital records supplements from 1620s | In-person; catalog at www.sec.state.ma.us/arc |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration study series, vital records abstracts | In-person / subscription at americanancestors.org |
| County registries of deeds | Original deed books from the 1630s | In-person at each county registry |
| County probate courts | Original wills, inventories, administrations from the 1630s | In-person at each county courthouse |
| Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston | Published transcriptions of colonial records, town histories | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting records (1620–1700): The one FamilySearch volume covering this period (image group 007612044) is browse-only — no name index, no full-text search.
- County court records (civil and criminal, 1630s–1700): Not systematically digitized or indexed for the colonial period.
- Plymouth Colony records: Published in multi-volume sets; check NEHGS and research libraries. Not fully searchable online.
- English departure records for Great Migration immigrants: Held in England (State Papers, port books); some accessible via Ancestry and FindMyPast English record collections.

## Known record losses
King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed town records, church registers, and local documents in many Massachusetts towns — particularly in the Connecticut River valley and central Massachusetts. No tool result in this survey pinpoints specific town registers lost. The Massachusetts Archives is the primary repository for surviving colonial-era records. Published town histories sometimes preserve transcriptions of records since lost.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts returned only generic content during this survey — they were not Massachusetts-specific. Consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy before relying on this guide's absence of their details.
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) is a separate jurisdiction. If your ancestor lived in Plymouth Colony towns before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records — published and indexed separately — before Massachusetts Bay records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), "Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately."
- The Great Migration study by Robert Charles Anderson (NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving in New England 1620–1643, with citations to primary sources — it is the starting point for any early Massachusetts ancestor.
- The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner–Corbin) abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns and is frequently the most accessible transcription of colonial vital records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- Town meeting and proprietors' records (FamilySearch volume 007612044, browse-only images, 188 images, 1620–1698) name inhabitants not found in surviving vital or church registers — essential for the colonial period.
- Congregational church admission records are distinct from baptismal registers: adult members were formally admitted to full communion, creating a separate dated record sometimes years after baptism; search both series.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

**Oklahoma & the Land Run of 1889 — Locality Guide**

Oklahoma was an almost entirely new place in 1889. Before the Land Run of April 22 that year, the western half was federally controlled **Unassigned Lands** with no county government, and the eastern half was **Indian Territory** governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under a separate federal framework. The most valuable records for Land Run-era families are:

**Key Record Types & Repositories**

- **Homestead Files** — the most direct source. Held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. under Record Group 49; partially searchable on FamilySearch and at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). These name the settler, their witnesses, and their proof of five years' continuous residence.
- **1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census** — the single most important early census source. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally, but the Oklahoma territorial census survives at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.
- **County marriages from 1890 onward** — searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Mission and church records (1820–1965)** — searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Indian Censuses and Rolls (1851–1959)** — essential for anyone with Five Civilized Tribes ancestry; searchable on FamilySearch.

**Two Critical Distinctions**

1. **Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory**: These were entirely separate jurisdictions until statehood in 1907. Which record series you search depends on exactly where your ancestor settled — western (Territory) or eastern (Indian Territory) Oklahoma.
2. **Follow the trail backward**: Most Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, or Missouri**. The paper trail before 1889 almost always runs through one of those departure states rather than Oklahoma itself.

**Next Steps**

Identify which part of Oklahoma your ancestor settled in and which county they lived in by 1900, then search the homestead files and the 1890 territorial census as the first documentary anchors. The guide has been saved to your project as **loc_001**.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Oklahoma (1880–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory organized May 2, 1890, by the Organic Act (from the Unassigned Lands opened April 22, 1889); Oklahoma became a state November 16, 1907, by merger of Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Guthrie was the territorial capital (1890–1907).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal (Unassigned Lands/Indian Territory before 1890); U.S. Territory (Oklahoma Territory, 1890–1907).
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this jurisdiction. The Land Run of April 22, 1889, drew approximately 50,000 participants to roughly 2 million acres (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889).
- **Economy:** Agricultural homesteading, cattle ranching; oil and gas discovery by the early 1900s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) in Indian Territory; Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons affiliated with the Five Civilized Tribes); African American settlers who established all-Black towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic, and other Protestant denominations; Five Civilized Tribes had established mission churches beginning in the 1820s–1840s.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889; subsequent land runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 (including the Cherokee Strip Run of 1893); Oklahoma and Indian Territory statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: The Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory under federal jurisdiction; no county-level civil government existed.
- May 2, 1890: Organic Act created Oklahoma Territory (western portion) with county government. Indian Territory (eastern portion, governed by Five Civilized Tribes) remained a **separate jurisdiction** throughout the territorial period.
- 1890–1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were two distinct jurisdictions with separate record systems. Families in what is now eastern Oklahoma generated records under Indian Territory / Five Civilized Tribes governance, not Oklahoma Territory county government.
- November 16, 1907: Statehood merged both territories into Oklahoma, unifying the record-keeping system.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma Territory county-level civil registration began after the Organic Act of 1890. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma returned only generic content during this survey — exact registration start dates could not be confirmed from tool results. Consult the Oklahoma Historical Society or Oklahoma State Archives before assuming records exist for specific years.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1890 onward — FamilySearch collection 2134789, "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (456,789 records / 913,578 persons, 228,394 images). Birth and death registration specifics for the territorial period were not confirmed by tool results.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Oklahoma State Archives; FamilySearch (marriages).
- **Gaps:** Civil registration in the Unassigned Lands before 1890 did not exist. Indian Territory had no county-level civil registration before 1907 — vital events for those families are found in mission/church registers and federal records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; homestead proof affidavits naming family members; 1890 territorial census.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Catholic missions operating in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward; Protestant denominational churches established in Oklahoma Territory towns beginning 1889.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records / 61,728 images). Denominational archives and local church offices hold originals.
- **Gaps:** Anglo-American Protestant congregations in new Oklahoma Territory towns began keeping records sporadically from 1889 (per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records); coverage is uneven for 1889–1900.
- **Language:** English; some earlier mission records may contain mixed-language or tribal-language entries.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory residents were enumerated separately in the 1900 federal census. The 1910 federal census covers Oklahoma as a state.
- **Territorial census (1890):** The Oklahoma Territory 1890 special/territorial census survives and is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society — one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations in the nation (per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). This is the most important early census source for Land Run settlers.
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records / 283,945 images), covers periodic enumerations of Five Civilized Tribes members — indexed + images.
- **Tax rolls (1890s):** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers and substitute for missing census years (per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Access:** Indian Censuses and Rolls are indexed + images on FamilySearch. The 1890 territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society may require in-person access or a written inquiry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, civil and criminal cases, and naturalization petitions.
- **Date range:** Oklahoma Territory district courts from 1890; Indian Territory courts (federal) from their establishment.
- **Where held:** Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). These include district court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records. Post-1907 records are at county courthouses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (public land state; land distributed via the General Land Office / Bureau of Land Management system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office administered homestead claims; land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher handled the 1889 run (per Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889). Patents were issued by the federal government after settlers proved five years of residence and improvement.
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates/patents, rejected applications, deeds, and county deed books.
- **Where held:** Homestead case files and land patents are at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office; per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Partially indexed on FamilySearch and at glorecords.blm.gov. FamilySearch collection 1541872, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 records / 117,283 images). Volume 005221388 (402 images, **74% name-indexed — indexed + images**) contains land-entry case files and homestead final proofs for 1889–1907.
- **Research value:** Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with named witnesses, and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can contain detailed family information.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War veterans were among the Land Run settlers; Spanish-American War (1898); World War I draft (1917–18) covers men who settled in Oklahoma after the runs.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files; WWI draft registration cards; Spanish-American War records.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds cemetery transcriptions for Oklahoma cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries and county courthouses; some early cemetery records may be undigitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New territorial towns quickly established newspapers beginning in 1889 (Guthrie, Kingfisher, and other settlements had papers within weeks of the land run).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical Oklahoma newspapers. The Oklahoma Historical Society and state university libraries hold microfilm of additional territorial-era papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage and arrival notices, legal notices, and homestead proof publication requirements (which mandated public announcement).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant origins:** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states — tracing origins requires searching departure-state records (per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions filed in territorial district courts (at National Archives at Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives) for foreign-born settlers; passenger lists for immigrant ancestors at NARA.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County-level property and poll tax rolls.
- **Date range:** From county organization beginning 1889–1890.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives and county courthouses.
- **Substitute value:** 1890s tax rolls are a critical substitute for the largely destroyed 1890 federal census.

### Other record types
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (1898–1910):** Essential for Five Civilized Tribes ancestry. FamilySearch volume 005221389 (176 images) is **browse-only — 0% name-indexed, must be examined image-by-image**. FamilySearch collection 1987432 covers the broader enrollment series.
- **Freedmen records:** Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons affiliated with the Five Civilized Tribes) are enumerated in Dawes Rolls and have dedicated enrollment jackets.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1541872: Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Collection 1987432: Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Collection 2134789: County Marriages, 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Collection 1654321: Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Land, Native American, marriage, and church records | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead records | Federal land patents not yet on FamilySearch | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1900 and 1910 federal census | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Civil War veterans, Spanish-American War | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Territorial-era newspapers, homestead notices | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Homestead case files (RG 49), territorial court records, naturalization | Free / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes matched the place and period in volume_search; both are detailed above. This was the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 territorial census; territorial records; county newspapers | In-person / online inquiry (okhistory.org) |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial and early state government records; county tax rolls | In-person / written request |
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory district court records (1890–1907), naturalization | In-person / written request |
| National Archives, Washington D.C. | General Land Office homestead case files (Record Group 49); military pension files | In-person / written request; some digitized |
| County courthouses | Post-1890 deeds, probate, marriages, and local records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Oklahoma Historical Society 1890 territorial census — may require in-person access or written inquiry.
- Territorial court civil and criminal case files (National Archives at Fort Worth) — some may require an in-person visit or written request.
- County-level tax rolls from the 1890s — largely physical or on microfilm at the Oklahoma State Archives.
- Early church registers from congregations established 1889–1900 in new towns — coverage is uneven; many originals remain at local churches or denominational archives.

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed nationally. The Oklahoma Territory 1890 special/territorial census survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society (per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run) — this is the most significant substitute.
- No tool result confirmed additional specific record losses for Oklahoma Territory for this period.

## Research tips
- **Search both jurisdictions before 1907.** Before statehood, Oklahoma Territory (western) and Indian Territory (eastern) were legally separate. A family in what is now eastern Oklahoma generated records under Indian Territory / federal governance — not Oklahoma Territory county courts. Determine which jurisdiction your ancestor lived in before choosing which record series to search.
- **Start with homestead files for Land Run settlers.** Each homestead file (Record Group 49, National Archives) includes the application, settlement proof affidavits with witness names, and the patent. Rejected applications also survive and are often more detailed. FamilySearch collection 1541872 and glorecords.blm.gov are the starting points. Volume 005221388 on FamilySearch (74% indexed) covers 1889–1907 homestead final proofs directly.
- **Use the 1890 territorial census.** This is a rare surviving 1890-era enumeration and the only early snapshot of settlers after the Land Run. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds it.
- **Trace origins in departure states.** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and neighboring states (per wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). When the Oklahoma record trail ends, search the state they left.
- **For Five Civilized Tribes ancestry, start with the Dawes Rolls.** The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (FamilySearch volume 005221389, browse-only) and the broader Indian Censuses and Rolls collection (1987432) are foundational. Freedmen and intermarried whites are also enrolled.
- **Naturalization records are in territorial courts.** Pre-1906 naturalizations for foreign-born settlers were filed in any court of record — Oklahoma Territory district court records at the National Archives at Fort Worth are the primary source.

Locality guide saved as loc_001.

---

Oklahoma was an almost entirely new place in 1889 — before the Land Run of April 22 that year, the western half was federally controlled Unassigned Lands with no county government, and the eastern half was Indian Territory governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under a separate federal framework. The most valuable records for Land Run-era families are the homestead files themselves (held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. under Record Group 49, partially searchable on FamilySearch and at glorecords.blm.gov), which name each settler, their witnesses, and their proof of five years' continuous residence. The surviving Oklahoma Territory 1890 territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is the single most important early census source, since the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally. County marriages from 1890 onward and mission and church records from 1820 through 1965 are searchable on FamilySearch, as are Indian Censuses and Rolls (1851–1959) for anyone with Five Civilized Tribes ancestry. Two warnings matter most: Oklahoma Territory (western half) and Indian Territory (eastern half) were entirely separate jurisdictions until statehood in 1907, so which record series to search depends on exactly where your ancestor lived; and because most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri, the trail back before 1889 almost always runs through one of those departure states rather than Oklahoma itself.

The next step is to identify which part of Oklahoma (Territory or Indian Territory) your ancestor settled in and which county they lived in by 1900, then search the homestead files and the 1890 territorial census as the first documentary anchors.

Here is the locality research guide for the Alabama region around 1800, before statehood:

---

## Alabama Region c. 1795–1820: Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Context

This period predates Alabama statehood (1819). The region passed through several jurisdictions:

- **Spanish rule** — the Mobile/coastal area remained under Spain until 1813
- **Mississippi Territory** — created 1798, encompassed most of present-day Alabama
- **Alabama Territory** — separated from Mississippi Territory in 1817, became a state in 1819

There was **no civil registration** of births and deaths in this period. Research relies on church registers, land records, territorial censuses, and tax lists.

---

### Record Types & What Survives

#### Land Records
- **Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** — available on FamilySearch; this is one of the richest sources for identifying settlers in the Alabama region before statehood.

#### Censuses & Tax Lists
- **Territorial censuses** for 1801, 1805, and 1808 exist as paper records held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery — **not currently online**.
- The **1810 Federal Census** has a name index on FamilySearch, but no images survive for Alabama (the original schedules were destroyed).

#### Church Records
- Some church registers survive from as early as 1803 on FamilySearch, though coverage is sparse for this early period.

#### Probate & County Records
- County marriage and probate records begin appearing from about 1809 on FamilySearch for the earliest-organized Alabama counties.

#### Spanish Colonial Records (Mobile Area)
- Records for the Mobile/coastal area under Spanish rule are held primarily at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with some copies at the **Library of Congress**. These are not currently available through FamilySearch.

---

### Digitized Browse Volumes (Unindexed Film)

A search specifically for digitized but non-name-indexed browsable FamilySearch film volumes for pre-1820 Alabama **returned no results**. No such browse-only volumes appear to be filed under Alabama for this period in FamilySearch's volume system.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Land records (1798+), some church records (1803+), county marriages/probate (1809+), 1810 census index |
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery** | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808), county records, state records |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville / Library of Congress** | Spanish colonial records for Mobile area, pre-1813 |

---

### Practical Next Steps

1. **Identify the specific county** — territorial records are organized by county, so knowing your ancestor's county of residence is essential.
2. **Search the Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records (1798–1907)** on FamilySearch — this is your best online starting point for locating settlers.
3. **Contact ADAH directly** for access to the territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808), which are not online.
4. For the Mobile/coastal area, factor in Spanish-era record-keeping and check Library of Congress holdings for colonial copies.
5. Consult the **FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy wiki page** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy for additional collection guidance.

---

*Survey covered the Alabama region from roughly 1795 to 1820. No unindexed browse-only volumes were found for this period on FamilySearch; the territorial-era gaps are significant and many records must be sought at ADAH or through specialized repositories.*

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1795-1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1798 as the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory; separated as Alabama Territory in 1817; admitted as the 22nd state in 1819.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial government was based at Natchez (the Mississippi portion). No single Alabama county seat until counties were organized during the territorial period.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798-1817), then Alabama Territory (1817-1819). Before 1798, the Mobile coastal area was under Spanish colonial rule (1780-1813), British rule before that (1763-1780), and French rule before that (1702-1763).
- **Population during period:** Population data for pre-statehood Alabama was not returned by the population tool during this survey.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, trading with the Creek and Cherokee nations.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations; Anglo-American settlers migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after the Creek War of 1813-1814); French and Spanish Creole population around Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area, from the French and Spanish colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuits beginning in the late 1790s-early 1800s; Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813-1814, which opened much of central Alabama to Anglo-American settlement; U.S. seizure of Spanish-held Mobile in 1813.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: Present-day Alabama was not under U.S. jurisdiction. The northern inland area was claimed by Georgia and Spain; the Mobile coastal zone was administered by Spain.
- 1798: Mississippi Territory established, encompassing most of present-day Mississippi and the southern strip of Alabama.
- 1804: Mississippi Territory expanded to include most of present-day Alabama.
- 1813: U.S. seized the Mobile District from Spain.
- 1817: Mississippi Territory divided; Alabama Territory created from the eastern portion.
- 1819: Alabama admitted as a state.
- Records created before 1819 were created under Mississippi Territory or Spanish/British colonial authority; they are not filed under "Alabama" in most archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration system existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama vital records returned only generic content during this survey and stated no Alabama-specific registration start year. The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy article confirms that territorial records consisted of land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records -- not civil vital registration.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records begin with county formation. FamilySearch collection 1598408 ("Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950," 612,345 records, 306,172 images) is the earliest Alabama marriage collection available. No birth or death registration system existed in the target period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598408 at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408 (indexed + images).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration existed around 1800. County marriage records begin only with county formation, the earliest in this FamilySearch collection being 1809.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (especially Catholic registers in the Mobile area); territorial census lists; estate inventories in probate records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, from the French and Spanish colonial period); Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian circuits arriving in the late 1790s-early 1800s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. For the Mobile area, Catholic registers survive from the colonial period and are especially important before 1803.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396 ("Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950," 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers from 1803; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396 (indexed + images). Spanish-era Catholic Mobile District records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress; French-era records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Gaps:** No FamilySearch church records specifically for 1795-1803 appear in the collection. The colonial-era Catholic records for the Mobile area are held at overseas archives (not online via FamilySearch). Church records for inland Alabama before 1803 are sparse.
- **Language:** Colonial-era Catholic records from the Spanish period are in Spanish; French-period records are in French.

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama; these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery -- they are NOT available online via FamilySearch. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering present-day Alabama was 1810. FamilySearch collection 2016756 ("Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890," 287,634 records) provides index access; this collection has no images. The original 1810 census images are on Ancestry.
- **Mississippi Territory census substitutes:** Collection 1927171 ("Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890," 198,340 records) covers the Mississippi Territory period and may include records relevant to present-day Alabama -- index only, no images.
- **Access:** Territorial censuses 1801-1808: physical records at ADAH. 1810 federal census: indexed on FamilySearch (no images in collection), images on Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1537764 ("Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985," 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins with 1809, coinciding with early county formation.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** Collection 1855293 ("Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920," 245,670 records, 122,835 images) covers the territorial period beginning 1799 -- images are available; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293.
- **Where held:** Alabama probate collection 1537764 at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764 (indexed + images).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the rectangular survey system. Original surveys were conducted during the territorial period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents for Alabama were issued through the federal General Land Office. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds the patent database; early territorial patents begin around 1800-1810.
- **Mississippi Territory land records:** Collection 1919694 ("Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907," 312,450 records, 156,225 images) begins in 1798 and covers the territorial period -- images are available. This is a critical resource for the target period; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694 (indexed + images).
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area exist at the Archivo General de Indias and the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** BLM GLO at glorecords.blm.gov; FamilySearch collection 1919694; original county deed books at Alabama county courthouses and ADAH.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812; various territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for Creek War and War of 1812 veterans); territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal service and pension records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many NARA military records (subscription). Territorial militia records are at ADAH.
- **Notes:** Bounty land warrants are especially relevant -- many early Alabama settlers received land as war veterans, and the warrants link families to specific land grants.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Alabama cemeteries. For the pre-statehood period, most burials were in family and church cemeteries without formal sexton records.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for established congregations (Catholic Mobile area) may survive at local church archives. Early Protestant burials often have no contemporary written record.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Few or no newspapers were published in the Alabama region around 1800. The territorial period saw sporadic publication primarily after county formation. This survey did not confirm any specific Alabama territorial newspaper titles from tool results.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspaper archives; coverage for pre-1820 Alabama is likely sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was a port of entry during the Spanish colonial period (1780-1813). New Orleans was the nearest major port for settlers arriving by water.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists to Mobile in the Spanish/French period (at overseas archives); naturalization records (filed in territorial and later county courts); Spanish colonial passport and emigration records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; territorial and colonial-era records at ADAH and overseas archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial-era tax lists; personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax records begin with county organization during the territorial period (after 1799 in the Mississippi Territory).
- **Where held:** Territorial tax records are at ADAH. Some may appear in collection 2016756 (the Alabama census substitutes) or collection 1927171 (Mississippi census substitutes, 1792-1890).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary census substitute for 1800-1809 events, since the federal census did not cover this area until 1810.

### Other record types
- **Territorial records:** Land grants, militia rolls, court minutes, and magistrate records were created under the Mississippi Territory government beginning 1798 and are held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Colonial records:** Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants; at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress. French colonial records (1702-1763) are at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (coll. 1598408; 306K images); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (coll. 1537764; 219K images); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (coll. 1986396; 78K images); Alabama, Compiled Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (coll. 2016756; index only); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907 (coll. 1919694; 156K images); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920 (coll. 1855293; 123K images); Mississippi, Compiled Census Substitutes, 1792-1890 (coll. 1927171; index only) | Marriage, probate, church, territorial land and court, and census records from 1798 onward | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1810 federal census images (not in FamilySearch collection) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO | glorecords.blm.gov | Federal land patents; records not in FamilySearch collections | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service and pension records for Creek War, War of 1812 veterans | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Federal service records, pension files, land patents, naturalization | Free / in-person |
| FindAGrave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery transcriptions where sexton records are absent | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes filed under "Alabama, United States" for the pre-1820 period (this was checked with and without year constraints). No browse-only image volumes for pre-statehood Alabama were found in the FamilySearch volume system. The indexed collections listed above DO include images for some record types from 1803 and 1809 onward.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808; territorial land, court, and militia records; county records | In-person; some digitized via ADAH website |

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1795-1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1798 as the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory; separated as Alabama Territory in 1817; admitted as the 22nd state in 1819.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial government was based at Natchez (the Mississippi portion). No single Alabama county seat until counties were organized during the territorial period.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798-1817), then Alabama Territory (1817-1819). Before 1798, the Mobile coastal area was under Spanish colonial rule (1780-1813), British rule before that (1763-1780), and French rule before that (1702-1763).
- **Population during period:** Population data for pre-statehood Alabama was not returned by the population tool during this survey.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, trading with the Creek and Cherokee nations.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations; Anglo-American settlers migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after the Creek War of 1813-1814); French and Spanish Creole population around Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area, from the French and Spanish colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuits beginning in the late 1790s-early 1800s; Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813-1814, which opened much of central Alabama to Anglo-American settlement; U.S. seizure of Spanish-held Mobile in 1813.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: Present-day Alabama was not under U.S. jurisdiction. The northern inland area was claimed by Georgia and Spain; the Mobile coastal zone was administered by Spain.
- 1798: Mississippi Territory established, encompassing most of present-day Mississippi and the southern strip of Alabama.
- 1804: Mississippi Territory expanded to include most of present-day Alabama.
- 1813: U.S. seized the Mobile District from Spain.
- 1817: Mississippi Territory divided; Alabama Territory created from the eastern portion.
- 1819: Alabama admitted as a state.
- Records created before 1819 were created under Mississippi Territory or Spanish/British colonial authority; they are not filed under "Alabama" in most archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration system existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama vital records returned only generic content during this survey and stated no Alabama-specific registration start year. The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy article confirms that territorial records consisted of land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records -- not civil vital registration.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records begin with county formation. FamilySearch collection 1598408 ("Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950," 612,345 records, 306,172 images) is the earliest Alabama marriage collection available. No birth or death registration system existed in the target period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598408 at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408 (indexed + images).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration existed around 1800. County marriage records begin only with county formation, the earliest in this FamilySearch collection being 1809.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (especially Catholic registers in the Mobile area); territorial census lists; estate inventories in probate records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, from the French and Spanish colonial period); Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian circuits arriving in the late 1790s-early 1800s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. For the Mobile area, Catholic registers survive from the colonial period and are especially important before 1803.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396 ("Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950," 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers from 1803; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396 (indexed + images). Spanish-era Catholic Mobile District records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress; French-era records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Gaps:** No FamilySearch church records specifically for 1795-1803 appear in the collection. The colonial-era Catholic records for the Mobile area are held at overseas archives (not online via FamilySearch). Church records for inland Alabama before 1803 are sparse.
- **Language:** Colonial-era Catholic records from the Spanish period are in Spanish; French-period records are in French.

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama; these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery -- they are NOT available online via FamilySearch. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering present-day Alabama was 1810. FamilySearch collection 2016756 ("Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890," 287,634 records) provides index access; this collection has no images. The original 1810 census images are on Ancestry.
- **Mississippi Territory census substitutes:** Collection 1927171 ("Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890," 198,340 records) covers the Mississippi Territory period and may include records relevant to present-day Alabama -- index only, no images.
- **Access:** Territorial censuses 1801-1808: physical records at ADAH. 1810 federal census: indexed on FamilySearch (no images in collection), images on Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1537764 ("Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985," 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins with 1809, coinciding with early county formation.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** Collection 1855293 ("Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920," 245,670 records, 122,835 images) covers the territorial period beginning 1799 -- images are available; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293.
- **Where held:** Alabama probate collection 1537764 at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764 (indexed + images).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the rectangular survey system. Original surveys were conducted during the territorial period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents for Alabama were issued through the federal General Land Office. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds the patent database; early territorial patents begin around 1800-1810.
- **Mississippi Territory land records:** Collection 1919694 ("Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907," 312,450 records, 156,225 images) begins in 1798 and covers the territorial period -- images are available. This is a critical resource for the target period; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694 (indexed + images).
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area exist at the Archivo General de Indias and the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** BLM GLO at glorecords.blm.gov; FamilySearch collection 1919694; original county deed books at Alabama county courthouses and ADAH.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812; various territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for Creek War and War of 1812 veterans); territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal service and pension records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many NARA military records (subscription). Territorial militia records are at ADAH.
- **Notes:** Bounty land warrants are especially relevant -- many early Alabama settlers received land as war veterans, and the warrants link families to specific land grants.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Alabama cemeteries. For the pre-statehood period, most burials were in family and church cemeteries without formal sexton records.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for established congregations (Catholic Mobile area) may survive at local church archives. Early Protestant burials often have no contemporary written record.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Few or no newspapers were published in the Alabama region around 1800. The territorial period saw sporadic publication primarily after county formation. This survey did not confirm any specific Alabama territorial newspaper titles from tool results.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspaper archives; coverage for pre-1820 Alabama is likely sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was a port of entry during the Spanish colonial period (1780-1813). New Orleans was the nearest major port for settlers arriving by water.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists to Mobile in the Spanish/French period (at overseas archives); naturalization records (filed in territorial and later county courts); Spanish colonial passport and emigration records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; territorial and colonial-era records at ADAH and overseas archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial-era tax lists; personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax records begin with county organization during the territorial period (after 1799 in the Mississippi Territory).
- **Where held:** Territorial tax records are at ADAH. Some may appear in collection 2016756 (the Alabama census substitutes) or collection 1927171 (Mississippi census substitutes, 1792-1890).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary census substitute for 1800-1809 events, since the federal census did not cover this area until 1810.

### Other record types

- **Colonial records:** Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants; at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress. - **Language:** Colonial-era Catholic records from the Spanish period are in Spanish; French-period records are in French.

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama; these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery -- they are NOT available online via FamilySearch. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering present-day Alabama was 1810. FamilySearch collection 2016756 ("Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890," 287,634 records) provides index access; this collection has no images. The original 1810 census images are on Ancestry.
- **Mississippi Territory census substitutes:** Collection 1927171 ("Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890," 198,340 records) covers the Mississippi Territory period and may include records relevant to present-day Alabama -- index only, no images.
- **Access:** Territorial censuses 1801-1808: physical records at ADAH. 1810 federal census: indexed on FamilySearch (no images in collection), images on Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1537764 ("Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985," 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins with 1809, coinciding with early county formation.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** Collection 1855293 ("Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920," 245,670 records, 122,835 images) covers the territorial period beginning 1799 -- images are available; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293.
- **Where held:** Alabama probate collection 1537764 at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764 (indexed + images).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state using the rectangular survey system. Original surveys were conducted during the territorial period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents for Alabama were issued through the federal General Land Office. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds the patent database; early territorial patents begin around 1800-1810.
- **Mississippi Territory land records:** Collection 1919694 ("Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907," 312,450 records, 156,225 images) begins in 1798 and covers the territorial period -- images are available. This is a critical resource for the target period; at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694 (indexed + images).
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area exist at the Archivo General de Indias and the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** BLM GLO at glorecords.blm.gov; FamilySearch collection 1919694; original county deed books at Alabama county courthouses and ADAH.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812; various territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for Creek War and War of 1812 veterans); territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal service and pension records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many NARA military records (subscription). Territorial militia records are at ADAH.
- **Notes:** Bounty land warrants are especially relevant -- many early Alabama settlers received land as war veterans, and the warrants link families to specific land grants.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Alabama cemeteries. For the pre-statehood period, most burials were in family and church cemeteries without formal sexton records.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for established congregations (Catholic Mobile area) may survive at local church archives. Early Protestant burials often have no contemporary written record.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Few or no newspapers were published in the Alabama region around 1800. The territorial period saw sporadic publication primarily after county formation. This survey did not confirm any specific Alabama territorial newspaper titles from tool results.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspaper archives; coverage for pre-1820 Alabama is likely sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was a port of entry during the Spanish colonial period (1780-1813). New Orleans was the nearest major port for settlers arriving by water.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists to Mobile in the Spanish/French period (at overseas archives); naturalization records (filed in territorial and later county courts); Spanish colonial passport and emigration records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; territorial and colonial-era records at ADAH and overseas archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial-era tax lists; personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax records begin with county organization during the territorial period (after 1799 in the Mississippi Territory).
- **Where held:** Territorial tax records are at ADAH. Some may appear in collection 2016756 (the Alabama census substitutes) or collection 1927171 (Mississippi census substitutes, 1792-1890).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary census substitute for 1800-1809 events, since the federal census did not cover this area until 1810.

### Other record types
- **Territorial records:** Land grants, militia rolls, court minutes, and magistrate records were created under the Mississippi Territory government beginning 1798 and are held at ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Colonial records:** Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants; at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress. French colonial records (1702-1763) are at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (coll. 1598408; 306K images); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (coll. 1537764; 219K images); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (coll. 1986396; 78K images); Alabama, Compiled Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (coll. 2016756; index only); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907 (coll. 1919694; 156K images); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920 (coll. 1855293; 123K images); Mississippi, Compiled Census Substitutes, 1792-1890 (coll. 1927171; index only) | Marriage, probate, church, territorial land and court, and census records from 1798 onward | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1810 federal census images (not in FamilySearch collection) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO | glorecords.blm.gov | Federal land patents; records not in FamilySearch collections | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service and pension records for Creek War, War of 1812 veterans | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Federal service records, pension files, land patents, naturalization | Free / in-person |
| FindAGrave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery transcriptions where sexton records are absent | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes filed under "Alabama, United States" for the pre-1820 period (this was checked with and without year constraints). No browse-only image volumes for pre-statehood Alabama were found in the FamilySearch volume system. The indexed collections listed above DO include images for some record types from 1803 and 1809 onward.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808; territorial land, court, and militia records; county records | In-person; some digitized via ADAH website |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish Mobile District records: census returns, church registers, land grants (1780-1813) | In-person; some microfilm at Library of Congress |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial Alabama records (1702-1763) | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial Mobile District records | In-person; some digitized |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records; local Mobile records | In-person |
| County courthouses | County deed books, court minutes, probate from county formation | In-person |
| NARA, Washington, DC / Atlanta, GA | Federal service/pension records, land patents, territorial government records | In-person; some online via Fold3 and Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, and 1808 (physical records at ADAH)
- Spanish Mobile District colonial records (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress)
- French colonial Alabama records (ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Early territorial militia rolls and magistrate records (ADAH)
- Church records before 1803 (the FamilySearch church collection begins 1803)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey confirmed specific record losses for pre-statehood Alabama. The absence of browse-only digitized volumes in the volume_search result is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. Some records may have been dispersed when political authority changed hands (French to British, British to Spanish, Spanish to U.S.), but the status of those records was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

## Research tips
- **Search Mississippi Territory records first.** Around 1800, Alabama was the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory. Territorial records filed under "Mississippi" or "Mississippi Territory" are the primary home for 1798-1817 events in present-day Alabama, alongside ADAH. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **For Mobile area families before 1813, work the Spanish colonial record series.** Spanish rule lasted 1780-1813; church registers and land grants from that period survive at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Use land records as family proxies.** Because no civil vital registration existed, federal land patents (at BLM GLO), territorial land grants (FamilySearch collection 1919694), and deed records at county courthouses are primary sources for identifying individuals and family relationships.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing censuses.** For 1800-1809, before the first federal enumeration, territorial tax lists at ADAH identify householders; some may appear in the census substitutes collections on FamilySearch.
- **The 1810 federal census is the first for this area.** The Alabama census substitutes collection (coll. 2016756) is an index with no images; images of the original 1810 census are available on Ancestry.
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Alabama returned only generic content during this survey.** The wiki_search tool returned content from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy -- visit that page directly for more detail on record types and repositories.

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860s–1890s)

**Primary county surveyed:** Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (the core of the anthracite region), with notes applicable to the broader five-county coal region.

---

### Key Finding: Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898)
The most important specialized resource for Irish coal-region ancestors is the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — roughly **41,000 colliery workers** drawn from company payroll books, often recording a worker's **parish of origin in Ireland**. This directly bridges the gap to Irish records. It is described on the FamilySearch Wiki:
👉 https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records

---

### Catholic Church Records — Critical Diocese Warning
Irish families in this region were overwhelmingly Catholic. The diocese boundaries matter:

| County | Diocese |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland | **Diocese of Philadelphia** (before 1868: all five anthracite counties were under Philadelphia; Diocese of Allentown from 1961) |
| Luzerne, Lackawanna | Diocese of Scranton (created 1868) |

> ⚠️ **A search directed to Scranton records will miss Schuylkill and Carbon County parishes entirely.**

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Holdings — Schuylkill County
Five digitized volumes exist, but **four of the five are browse-only** with no name index. Irish surnames will not surface in a keyword search — these must be found by scrolling through images page by page.

---

### Five Anthracite Coal Counties
The full research region spans:
1. **Schuylkill** (surveyed — locality entry written as `loc_001`)
2. **Luzerne**
3. **Lackawanna**
4. **Northumberland**
5. **Carbon**

The other four counties still need their own locality surveys before a complete research plan can be built.

---

### Next Steps Recommended
- Use the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** to identify specific colliery employers and Irish parish of origin.
- Browse unindexed FamilySearch volumes for Schuylkill County page by page (search-images agent).
- Check Catholic vital records under the **Diocese of Philadelphia** for Schuylkill/Carbon/Northumberland parishes.
- Expand the locality survey to the remaining four counties.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Schuylkill County (1860–1900)

This guide focuses on Schuylkill County as the primary anthracite county and the county of death for the subject person. The other anthracite counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon — each require their own locality survey.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880); 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; mine operators, colliery workers (loaders, breaker boys, mule drivers), and service industries
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish immigration from the 1840s famine era onward; also Welsh, German, and from the 1880s Eastern European miners
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (served Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities); Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Anthracite coal boom mid-century; Molly Maguires labor unrest 1860s–1877; major strikes throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County formed 1811; boundaries stable across 1860–1900.
- **Lackawanna County** was split from **Luzerne County** in 1878. For the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre corridor, search Luzerne County records before 1878 and Lackawanna County records from 1878 onward.
- **Diocese boundary change, 1868:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties fell under the Catholic Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna passed to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg. Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for the Pennsylvania Vital Records page during this survey; specific statewide registration start dates by level cannot be confirmed from tool results. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317) covers deaths starting 1906 with 4,218,763 indexed records with images — **indexed + images**.
- **What exists:** Statewide death certificates from 1906 (collection 2255317). County-level marriage records in collection 1921317 "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, indexed + images). Civil marriages 1677–1950 in collection 1571957 (312,045 records). One **browse-only** volume of Schuylkill County marriage records (image group 007936753, 1870–1910, 94 images, 0% indexed — must be browsed image-by-image).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County clerk's office (Pottsville) for local originals; Pennsylvania State Archives for statewide series; FamilySearch for digitized collections.
